points.name: Be: am / is / are
points.can_do: Says who or what somebody is, how they feel and where they are; makes the negative and the question by moving or negating be.
points.typical_errors: BE: *I really happy*; *Do you tired?* for *Are you tired?*
points.sources: TE A1: Present simple of be · EGP: A1 (be + complement; negation of main verb be) · Not in Murphy EGiU (intermediate); Essential Grammar in Use units 1-2 (from memory, not checked)

points.name: Present simple: I work, she works
points.can_do: Talks about habits, routines and facts; adds -s / -es / -ies for he, she, it.
points.typical_errors: 3S: *She work here*; BE-VERB: *I am agree, I am live in Riga*
points.sources: Murphy 2 · TE A1: Present simple · EGP: A1 (affirmative; habits and general facts)

points.name: Present simple: don't / doesn't, Do / Does …?
points.can_do: Makes negatives and questions with do / does and keeps the main verb in the base form.
points.typical_errors: DO: *You like coffee? I not like it*; BASE: *She doesn't likes, Does she works?*
points.sources: Murphy 2 · TE A1: Present simple · EGP: A1 negative; A2 questions

points.name: Present continuous: am / is / are + -ing
points.can_do: Says what is happening at the moment of speaking, with negatives, questions and short answers; spells the -ing form.
points.typical_errors: BE: *I working now, She is work*; short answer *Yes, I'm*
points.sources: Murphy 1 · TE A1: Present continuous · EGP: A1 affirmative, events in progress; A2 negative, questions

points.name: Present simple or continuous: habit or now
points.can_do: Chooses between a habit (every day, usually) and an action in progress (now, at the moment, Look!).
points.typical_errors: NOW-HABIT: *Look! It rains. I am going to the gym every day*
points.sources: Murphy 3 · TE A1: Present simple or continuous; A2: Present simple vs present continuous · EGP: A1-A2 (both forms)

points.name: Present continuous: temporary situations and changes
points.can_do: Talks about something temporary around now (this week, these days) and about a change in progress (is getting better).
points.typical_errors: NOW-HABIT: *I work from home this week* for a temporary situation
points.sources: Murphy 1, 3 · TE A2: Present simple vs present continuous · EGP: A2 temporary situations; B1 temporary repeated actions

points.name: State verbs stay simple: know, like, want, need
points.can_do: Uses the simple form with verbs of knowing, liking, wanting and needing, also for something true right now.
points.typical_errors: STATE-ING: *I am knowing, I am wanting, I am needing help*
points.sources: Murphy 4 · TE A2: Stative vs dynamic verbs · EGP: A2 mental process verbs with the present simple

points.name: Verbs with two meanings: think, have, see, taste, be
points.can_do: Chooses simple or continuous by meaning: I think it's good (opinion) / I'm thinking about it (considering); She has a car / She's having lunch; He's being rude.
points.typical_errors: *I am thinking it is a good idea*; *I have a shower* for now
points.sources: Murphy 4 · TE B1: Present simple or present continuous · EGP: B1 mental process verbs

points.name: Always + continuous: an annoying habit
points.can_do: Shows irritation about something that happens too often: He's always losing his keys.
points.typical_errors: *He always loses his keys!* is correct but neutral; the continuous adds the annoyance
points.sources: Murphy 3 · TE B1: Present simple or present continuous (from memory); returns in C1: Advanced present simple and continuous · EGP: A2 present continuous with adverbs of indefinite frequency (form only)

points.name: Have got and have
points.can_do: Talks about possession with have got / have; makes the negative and question of each (I haven't got / I don't have).
points.typical_errors: *Do you have got? I haven't a car*; *I'm having a car*
points.sources: Murphy 17 · TE A1: Have got · EGP: A2 (auxiliary have; have got to)

points.name: The imperative: Open the door. Don't worry. Let's go.
points.can_do: Gives instructions, directions and suggestions with the base form, don't + base form and let's.
points.typical_errors: *Don't to worry; No smoke here; Let's to go*
points.sources: TE A1: The imperative · EGP: A2 affirmative, negative, let's · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Would like: I'd like …, Would you like …?
points.can_do: Asks for things and offers them politely; follows would like with a noun or to + verb.
points.typical_errors: *I would like go; Do you like a coffee?* as an offer; *I like to order* for *I'd like to order*
points.sources: Murphy 37, 58 · TE A1: Would you like…? I'd like… · EGP: A1 would like: wishes, invitations

points.name: There is / are, there was / were
points.can_do: Says that something exists or is somewhere; chooses is or are by the noun; asks Is there…? Are there…?
points.typical_errors: IT-THERE: *In my town is a park. There is two cafés. It is a park near here*
points.sources: Murphy 84 · TE A1: There is / are, there was / were · EGP: A1 there is, there are; A2 + uncountable, a lot of · Mentioned on the agreement card (there is + one, there are + more than one)

points.name: There or it
points.can_do: Uses there to introduce something new and it to talk about it again, or for weather, time and distance: There's a café. It's very good. It's cold.
points.typical_errors: IT-THERE: *Is cold today. There is cold. It is a problem with my phone*
points.sources: Murphy 84 · TE A1: There or it · EGP: A1-A2 (there is / are)

points.name: This, that, these, those
points.can_do: Points at things near and far, singular and plural, before a noun or alone, and goes on with it, not this, once the thing is known: This is my desk. It's new.
points.typical_errors: *This shoes; these book; that are my friends; A: What is this? B: This is a present* for *It is a present*
points.sources: TE A1: This, that, these, those; A1: This or it · EGP: A1 determiners; A2 pronouns · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Was / were
points.can_do: Talks about where somebody was and how things were; makes negatives and questions without did.
points.typical_errors: *Did you were there? I were tired. They was late*
points.sources: Murphy 5 · TE A1: Was / were · EGP: A1 past simple affirmative (be)

points.name: Past simple: regular verbs (-ed)
points.can_do: Tells about finished actions at a finished time (yesterday, last week, two days ago); spells -ed forms.
points.typical_errors: PAST-FORM: *Robert join us last week*; spelling *stoped, studyed*; *before two days* for *two days ago*
points.sources: Murphy 5, App. 1, App. 6 · TE A1: Past simple: regular and irregular · EGP: A1 affirmative (limited range); A2 increasing range

points.name: Past simple: irregular verbs
points.can_do: Uses the past forms of the common irregular verbs (went, saw, had, bought, took …).
points.typical_errors: PAST-FORM: *I buyed, she goed, he taked*
points.sources: Murphy 5, App. 1 · TE A1: Past simple: regular and irregular · EGP: A2 affirmative

points.name: Past simple: didn't, Did …?
points.can_do: Makes negatives and questions with did and returns the main verb to the base form.
points.typical_errors: BASE: *Did you went? I didn't saw it*; DO: *Where you went?*
points.sources: Murphy 5 · TE A1: Past simple: negatives and questions · EGP: A2 questions, negative

points.name: Used to + verb: past habits and states
points.can_do: Talks about what was true or regular in the past and is not now; didn't use to, Did you use to…?
points.typical_errors: *I use to get up at seven* for a present habit; *I didn't used to* (the spelling: Murphy gives didn't use to; EGP records both); *I used to went*
points.sources: Murphy 18 · TE A2: Used to · EGP: B1 (no longer true; negative didn't use to / didn't used to) · Level: test-english A2, EGP B1 (learners use it one level later than the list teaches it)

points.name: Used to or past simple; usually for the present
points.can_do: Keeps used to for repeated or lasting past situations, the past simple for one finished event, and usually + present simple for a present habit.
points.typical_errors: *We used to go to Rome last year; I use to drink coffee every morning*
points.sources: Murphy 18 · TE B1: Usually, used to, be used to, get used to · EGP: B1

points.name: Be used to and get used to + noun / -ing
points.can_do: Says that something is normal for somebody now, or is becoming normal: I'm used to getting up early. You'll get used to it.
points.typical_errors: *I'm used to get up early; I used to getting up early; I'm use to it*
points.sources: Murphy 61 · TE B1: Usually, used to, be used to, get used to; B1+: Used to, be used to, get used to · EGP: B1-B2 (not a separate EGP entry)

points.name: Would for past habits (not states)
points.can_do: Uses would + verb for repeated past actions in a story and used to for past states: We would play outside every day. I used to have a dog.
points.typical_errors: *I would have a dog when I was a child; I would live in Riga*
points.sources: Murphy 36 · TE B1+: Would and used to; B2: Narrative tenses, used to, would · EGP: B2 would: habitual past · On the used_to card only as a Watch out point

points.name: No longer, any more, any longer
points.can_do: Says that a situation has ended: I no longer smoke. I don't smoke any more.
points.typical_errors: *I don't smoke no more; I no longer don't work there; I any more live there*
points.sources: Murphy 111 · TE A2: No longer, anymore · EGP: B1 negation with adverbs · On the used_to card only as a Watch out point

points.name: Past continuous: was / were + -ing
points.can_do: Says what was in progress at a time in the past: At eight I was having breakfast.
points.typical_errors: BE: *I was work*; *They was waiting*; STATE-ING: *I was knowing her*
points.sources: Murphy 6 · TE A2: Past continuous and past simple · EGP: A2 affirmative, events in progress, background

points.name: Past continuous with past simple: when, while
points.can_do: Tells that a short action happened in the middle of a longer one: I was cooking when he called. He called while I was cooking.
points.typical_errors: BACKGROUND: *When you called, I watched TV*; *While I cooked, he was calling*
points.sources: Murphy 6 · TE A2: Past continuous and past simple · EGP: A2 past simple with when; past continuous background events

points.name: One after another or in the middle? When + past simple / continuous
points.can_do: Hears the difference: When Marta came in, we ate (then) / we were eating (already started); uses the past simple for complete and repeated actions.
points.typical_errors: *I was going there three times; We were walking home after the concert* for a complete action
points.sources: Murphy 6 · TE B1: Past simple, past continuous, past perfect · EGP: B1 ordering of past events; past continuous: repeated events

points.name: Two actions in progress; the background of a story
points.can_do: Sets the scene of a story and describes two things going on at the same time: It was raining, and people were hurrying home.
points.typical_errors: *While I was cooking, he watched TV* where both were in progress
points.sources: Murphy 6 · TE B1: Past simple, past continuous, past perfect · EGP: A2 background events; B1 past continuous: reason

points.name: The third form (past participle) of regular and irregular verbs
points.can_do: Knows the third form of the common verbs (done, seen, gone, written, made, built) and that regular verbs repeat -ed.
points.typical_errors: PAST-FORM: *I have went, she has saw, it was build, it is speak*
points.sources: Murphy App. 1 · TE A2: Present perfect; A2: Present and past simple passive · EGP: A2 (present perfect affirmative; passive affirmative)

points.name: Present perfect: have / has + third form
points.can_do: Forms the present perfect with negatives, questions and short answers: I've finished. She hasn't called. Have you seen it?
points.typical_errors: *She have finished; I has seen; Did you have seen?*
points.sources: Murphy 7 · TE A2: Present perfect · EGP: A2 affirmative, negative, questions

points.name: Present perfect for experience: ever, never, before
points.can_do: Asks and tells about life experience without saying when: Have you ever been to Rome? I have never tried it.
points.typical_errors: FINISHED-TIME: *I have been there in 2019*; *Did you ever be…?*; *I never have seen*
points.sources: Murphy 8 · TE A2: Present perfect · EGP: A2 experiences

points.name: Been or gone
points.can_do: Uses been for a visit that is over and gone for somebody who is still away: She's been to Paris. She's gone to Paris.
points.typical_errors: *He's gone to Rome twice; She's been to the shop* for somebody still out
points.sources: Murphy 7 · TE A2: Present perfect · EGP: A2 (not a separate EGP entry)

points.name: Present perfect with just, already, yet
points.can_do: Gives news and says whether something has happened: I've just finished. She's already left. Have you eaten yet?
points.typical_errors: *I already have eaten; I didn't finish yet; Have you yet eaten?*
points.sources: Murphy 7 · TE A2: Present perfect · EGP: A2 with yet; B1 with already; B1 recent past

points.name: Present perfect with for and since: up to now
points.can_do: Says how long a state has lasted up to now: I've known her for ten years / since school; asks How long have you…?
points.typical_errors: DURATION: *I live here for 10 years. I know him since 2015. I've lived here from 2015. How long are you here?*
points.sources: Murphy 11, 12 · TE A2: Present perfect; B1: For, since, from · EGP: A2 time with for; B1 duration with since; B1 unfinished

points.name: Present perfect or past simple: is the time finished?
points.can_do: Uses the past simple with a finished time (yesterday, in 2019, ago, When…?) and the present perfect when the time is not said or not finished.
points.typical_errors: FINISHED-TIME: *I have seen him yesterday. When have you arrived? Who has invented the telephone?*
points.sources: Murphy 13, 14 · TE A2: Present perfect or past simple; B1: Past simple or present perfect · EGP: A2 present perfect: experiences; past simple with time adjuncts

points.name: Still true or finished? News and details; today, this week
points.can_do: Chooses by the link with now: I've taught here since 2015 / I taught there from 2009 to 2015; gives news in the present perfect and the details in the past simple; uses the present perfect with a period that is not over (today, this week).
points.typical_errors: *I've taught there from 2009 to 2015; A: I've cut my finger. B: How have you done that?; When have you arrived?* for the details after the news
points.sources: Murphy 13, 14 · TE B1: Past simple or present perfect · EGP: B1 unfinished; recent past

points.name: Superlative + present perfect: the best film I've ever seen
points.can_do: Combines a superlative with ever and the present perfect to rank an experience.
points.typical_errors: *It's the best film I ever saw; the best film I've never seen*
points.sources: Murphy 8, 108 · TE B1: Comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs (from memory) · EGP: B1 present perfect with superlative; superlative: the best with noun and present perfect

points.name: Present perfect continuous: have been + -ing
points.can_do: Talks about an activity that started in the past and is still going on, with for, since and How long: I've been waiting for an hour.
points.typical_errors: DURATION: *I am waiting for an hour. How long are you learning English?*; *She has been work all day*
points.sources: Murphy 9, 11 · TE B1: Present perfect simple and continuous · EGP: B1 affirmative, questions; single continuing event

points.name: Present perfect continuous: a recent activity you can see
points.can_do: Explains a present situation by a recent activity: You're out of breath. Have you been running?
points.typical_errors: *You are out of breath. Did you run? / Have you run?* where the activity, not its completion, is meant
points.sources: Murphy 9 · TE B1: Present perfect simple and continuous · EGP: B2 present perfect continuous: recent past

points.name: Present perfect simple or continuous: how much or how long?
points.can_do: Chooses the simple form for a finished amount or result (I've read three chapters) and the continuous for the activity and its length (I've been reading all afternoon); keeps state verbs simple (I've known him for years).
points.typical_errors: *I've been reading three chapters. I've been knowing him for years. How long have you had been…?*
points.sources: Murphy 10, 11 · TE B1: Present perfect simple and continuous; B1+: Present perfect simple or continuous · EGP: B1 present perfect continuous: repeated continuing events

points.name: It's the first time I've …
points.can_do: Uses the present perfect after It's the first / second time: It's the first time I've driven a car.
points.typical_errors: *It's the first time I drive a car; It's the first time I am here*
points.sources: Murphy 8 · TE no line in the lists · EGP: not found in EGP · Standard point from Murphy unit 8; no content and no list line

points.name: Already, still, yet
points.can_do: Places and chooses the three words: She still hasn't called. He's already here. Is it ready yet? I'm still waiting.
points.typical_errors: *I still didn't finish* for *I still haven't finished; She yet hasn't called; He is here already?* as surprise
points.sources: Murphy 111 · TE B1+: Already, still, yet · EGP: B2 present perfect with still; B1 with already

points.name: Past perfect: had + third form, the earlier past
points.can_do: Shows which of two past actions happened first: When I got to the station, the train had left.
points.typical_errors: *When I arrived, the film has already started; She had went home; I have never seen snow before I moved*
points.sources: Murphy 15 · TE A2: Past perfect; B1: Past simple, past continuous, past perfect · EGP: B1 affirmative, negative; time up to then · Level: test-english A2, EGP B1, the app teaches it at B1.2. Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B1; the A2.2 path step is not needed.

points.name: Past perfect or past simple: is the order already clear?
points.can_do: Uses the past simple for actions told in the order they happened and with before / after when the order is clear; keeps the past perfect for stepping back.
points.typical_errors: *She had opened the door and had gone in; After I had breakfast I had gone to work*
points.sources: Murphy 15 · TE B1: Past simple, past continuous, past perfect · EGP: B1 past simple: ordering of past events

points.name: By the time, already, just, never … before with the past perfect
points.can_do: Uses the time words that go with the earlier past: By the time we arrived, the shop had closed. I had never seen snow before.
points.typical_errors: *By the time we arrived, the shop closed / has closed; I never saw snow before I moved*
points.sources: Murphy 15, 120 · TE B1: Past simple, past continuous, past perfect · EGP: B1 past perfect with adverbs

points.name: Narrative tenses: past simple, past continuous, past perfect together
points.can_do: Tells a story with events (past simple), background (past continuous) and what had happened before (past perfect), choosing all three in one text.
points.typical_errors: *When I have got home, I found the door open; I didn't go to the cinema. I have already seen the film*
points.sources: Murphy 6, 15 · TE B1: Past simple, past continuous, past perfect; B1+: Narrative tenses · EGP: B1 (all three forms)

points.name: Past perfect continuous: had been + -ing
points.can_do: Says how long an activity had been going on before a moment in the past: We'd been playing for half an hour when it started to rain.
points.typical_errors: *When it started to rain, we have been playing for half an hour; She had been work all day; We had been knowing each other*
points.sources: Murphy 16 · TE B1+: Narrative tenses; B2: Narrative tenses, used to, would · EGP: B1 affirmative, continuing events in the past; B2 negative, results

points.name: Had been doing, was doing or had done?
points.can_do: Chooses between an activity in progress at that moment (was doing), an activity before it (had been doing) and a finished amount before it (had done).
points.typical_errors: *The ground was wet because it was raining* (it had stopped); *By lunchtime she'd been writing ten emails*
points.sources: Murphy 16 · TE B2: Narrative tenses, used to, would · EGP: B2 past perfect continuous: results, background information

points.name: Will / won't + verb: predictions and what I think will happen
points.can_do: Talks about the future with will and won't, often after I think / I'm sure / probably; asks Will you…?
points.typical_errors: MODAL: *I will to help; It will rains; She wills*; *I think I won't* for *I don't think I'll*
points.sources: Murphy 21, 22 · TE A1: Will and shall · EGP: A1 affirmative; A2 negative, questions; B1 predictions

points.name: Shall I …? Shall we …?
points.can_do: Offers help and suggests doing something together: Shall I open the window? Shall we go?
points.typical_errors: *Will I open the window?* as an offer; *Shall we to go?*
points.sources: Murphy 21, 22 · TE A1: Will and shall · EGP: A2 offers and suggestions with shall

points.name: Be going to: plans and intentions
points.can_do: Says what somebody has decided to do: I'm going to visit my aunt this weekend; negatives and questions.
points.typical_errors: BE: *She going to call you; I'm going visit; I going to*
points.sources: Murphy 20 · TE A1: Be going to · EGP: A2 affirmative, questions, intentions

points.name: Will for a decision made now: offers, promises, requests
points.can_do: Reacts at the moment of speaking: I'm thirsty. I'll have some water. I'll help you. I won't tell anyone.
points.typical_errors: FUTURE: *I call you tomorrow* as a promise; *I'm going to answer it* as an instant decision; *I help you*
points.sources: Murphy 21, 23 · TE A2: Will vs be going to · EGP: A2 willingness, offers; requests with will

points.name: Will or going to
points.can_do: Chooses going to for a plan made before and for a prediction from what we can see now (Look at those clouds. It's going to rain), will for a decision made now and for what we think.
points.typical_errors: *I will visit my aunt this weekend* for an existing plan; *Look out! You will fall* with present evidence
points.sources: Murphy 23 · TE A2: Will vs be going to · EGP: A2 going to: intentions, predictions; B1 will: predictions

points.name: Present continuous for arrangements
points.can_do: Talks about a fixed arrangement with a time and usually other people: I'm meeting Anna at six tomorrow.
points.typical_errors: FUTURE: *I meet Anna tomorrow at six; I will meet the dentist at ten* for an appointment
points.sources: Murphy 19 · TE A2: Present continuous for arrangements · EGP: A2 future arrangements

points.name: Present simple for timetables and programmes
points.can_do: Uses the present simple for a fixed timetable: The train leaves at 7.15. The film starts at eight.
points.typical_errors: *The train will leave at 7.15* for a timetable
points.sources: Murphy 19 · TE B1: Future forms (from memory) · EGP: A2 present simple: timetables and plans

points.name: Future time clauses: when, as soon as, until, before, after + present
points.can_do: Keeps the present simple after the time word when talking about the future: I'll call you when I arrive.
points.typical_errors: TIME-CLAUSE: *When I will come home, I'll call you. I'll wait until she will come*
points.sources: Murphy 25 · TE A2: First conditional and future time clauses; B1: First conditional, future time clauses · EGP: A2 present simple with when; B1 with as soon as

points.name: When I do or when I've done; if and when
points.can_do: Uses the present perfect after when / after / as soon as / until to show that one action will be complete first: I'll call you when I've finished.
points.typical_errors: *When I will have finished; I'll call you when I finished*
points.sources: Murphy 25 · TE B1+: When I do / when I have done · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: Future forms: choosing among will, going to, present continuous, present simple
points.can_do: Chooses the right future form in one conversation: plan, arrangement, timetable, prediction, instant decision.
points.typical_errors: FUTURE: one form (will, or the present) for every future meaning
points.sources: Murphy 19, 20, 21, 22, 23 · TE B1: Future forms · EGP: B1 (all forms)

points.name: Future continuous: will be doing
points.can_do: Says what will be in progress at a future time: This time tomorrow I'll be flying to Rome.
points.typical_errors: *This time tomorrow I will fly; I will be fly; I will flying*
points.sources: Murphy 24 · TE B1+: Future continuous and future perfect · EGP: A2 affirmative with will; B1 negative; B2 questions, politeness

points.name: Future perfect: will have done
points.can_do: Says what will be complete before a future time: By Friday I'll have finished the report.
points.typical_errors: *By Friday I will finish* where completion before then is meant; *I will have finish; Until Friday I'll have finished*
points.sources: Murphy 24 · TE B1+: Future continuous and future perfect · EGP: B2 affirmative, negative; events completed in the future · Level: the B1+ list covers B1.2-B2.1; EGP B2, so the second half

points.name: Future perfect continuous: will have been doing
points.can_do: Says how long something will have lasted at a future time: In May I'll have been working here for ten years.
points.typical_errors: *In May I will work here for ten years; I'll have been work*
points.sources: TE B2: Future forms (from memory) · EGP: B2 affirmative, negative; looking back from a point in the future · Not in Murphy EGiU; Hewings, Advanced Grammar in Use (from memory, not checked)

points.name: Be about to, be due to, be to
points.can_do: Talks about the immediate future (about to), a scheduled event (due to) and an official arrangement or instruction (is to).
points.typical_errors: *I'm about leaving; The train is due arrive; I'm about to leave tomorrow*
points.sources: TE B2: Be about to, be due to · EGP: B2 be about to, be due to, be to · be about to is in Murphy Appendix 3 (from memory); be due to / be to are not in EGiU

points.name: Future in the past: was going to, would, was about to
points.can_do: Talks about a plan or expectation seen from a past moment: I was going to call you, but I forgot. I knew it would rain.
points.typical_errors: *I was going to called; I thought it will rain; I knew he is going to be late*
points.sources: Murphy 20 · TE B2: Future in the past · EGP: B1 be going to, would: future in the past; B2 be about to, be on the point of · On the past_continuous card (form line and Watch out). Level: test-english B2, EGP B1

points.name: Likely, bound, sure to; probably and definitely with will
points.can_do: Says how sure a future event is: She's likely to win. It's bound to rain. He'll probably come. He probably won't come.
points.typical_errors: *She is likely win; It's probably that; He won't probably come; It is bound raining*
points.sources: TE B1+: Likely, bound, probably · EGP: B2 be likely to: probability; be bound to: certainty; be sure / certain to · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Can / can't: ability, permission, requests
points.can_do: Says what somebody can do and asks for things: I can swim. Can I sit here? Can you help me?; no -s, no to, no do.
points.typical_errors: MODAL: *I can to swim; She cans drive; Do you can swim? He doesn't can*
points.sources: Murphy 26, 37 · TE A1: Can, can't · EGP: A1 affirmative, negative, questions; ability, requests; A2 permission

points.name: Could / couldn't: ability in the past
points.can_do: Talks about general ability in the past: I could swim when I was five. I couldn't sleep.
points.typical_errors: *I can swim when I was five; I could to swim; Did you could?*
points.sources: Murphy 26 · TE A2: Have to, don't have to, must, mustn't (the card of the topic); B1: Can, could, be able to · EGP: A2 could: ability

points.name: Polite requests and permission: Could you …? Can I …? Would you …?
points.can_do: Asks somebody to do something and asks for permission with the right degree of politeness.
points.typical_errors: *Could you to help me? Can you help me, please?* said to a stranger where *Could you* fits; *May you help me?*
points.sources: Murphy 37 · TE no line of its own (A1: Can; A1: Would you like) · EGP: A1 can: requests; A2 could: requests; B1 would: polite requests

points.name: Must and have to: obligation
points.can_do: Says what is necessary; forms have to with do / does (Do you have to go? She has to work).
points.typical_errors: MODAL: *We must to go; She musts; Do you must?*; *She have to; Has she to go?*
points.sources: Murphy 31 · TE A2: Have to, don't have to, must, mustn't · EGP: A2 must: obligation; A2 have to: affirmative, questions

points.name: Mustn't or don't have to
points.can_do: Separates not allowed (mustn't) from not necessary (don't have to).
points.typical_errors: *You mustn't come* meaning it is not necessary; *You don't have to smoke here* meaning it is forbidden
points.sources: Murphy 31, 32 · TE A2: Have to, don't have to, must, mustn't · EGP: A2 must: negative; have to: negative

points.name: Should / shouldn't: advice
points.can_do: Gives and asks for advice: You should see a doctor. What should I do?
points.typical_errors: MODAL: *You should to go; He shoulds; Do I should?*
points.sources: Murphy 33 · TE A2: Should · EGP: A2 affirmative, negative, questions; advice

points.name: Obligation in the past and future: had to, will have to
points.can_do: Moves obligation to other times, where must has no form: I had to work late yesterday. We'll have to leave early.
points.typical_errors: *I must work late yesterday; I musted; We will must leave; Did you had to?*
points.sources: Murphy 31 · TE B1: Have to, must, should · EGP: B1 have to: infinitive

points.name: Might and may: possibility
points.can_do: Says that something is possible now or in the future: It might rain. She may be late. They might not come.
points.typical_errors: MODAL: *It might rains; It mights; It might to rain; Maybe it will might*
points.sources: Murphy 29, 30 · TE A2: Might; A2: May and might · EGP: A2 may, might: possibility · Level: test-english A2, EGP A2; the app has its tasks at B1.1-B1.2 Decided by the teacher, 13 November: A2.2, as in the list; A2.2 tasks are to be written.

points.name: Be able to in other tenses
points.can_do: Uses be able to where can has no form: I'll be able to come. I haven't been able to call. I'd like to be able to swim.
points.typical_errors: MODAL: *I will can come; I haven't could call; I'd like to can swim*
points.sources: Murphy 26 · TE B1: Can, could, be able to · EGP: A2 will be able to; B1 modal with be able to; be able to: past

points.name: Could or was able to / managed to: one success
points.can_do: Uses was able to or managed to for one achievement in the past, could for general ability, couldn't for both.
points.typical_errors: COULD: *The door was locked, but I could open it; I could finish the report yesterday*
points.sources: Murphy 26 · TE B1: Can, could, be able to · EGP: B1 be able to: past

points.name: Permission: can, could, be allowed to
points.can_do: Talks about what is and was permitted, in any tense: We aren't allowed to park here. I was allowed to leave early.
points.typical_errors: *We are allowed park here; It is not allowed to smoke* with it
points.sources: Murphy 26, 37 · TE B2: Modals: permission, obligation, prohibition, necessity · EGP: B1 be allowed to: permission; could: permission · Level: taught by the app at B1 (EGP B1); the list names it at B2 as part of a wider set

points.name: Ought to and had better
points.can_do: Gives advice with ought to and a strong warning with had better (not) + base form: You'd better hurry.
points.typical_errors: *You ought go; You had better to go; You'd better don't; You better had*
points.sources: Murphy 33, 35 · TE B1: Had better, it's time · EGP: B1 ought to: advice (had better not found in EGP)

points.name: Deduction about the present: must, might, could, can't + be
points.can_do: Says how sure a guess is: He must be at home. She might be ill. That can't be right.
points.typical_errors: *She mustn't be at home* for *can't be*; *He can be at home* for *might be*; *It must to be*
points.sources: Murphy 28, 29 · TE B1: Modal verbs of deduction · EGP: B1 must: deductions and conclusions; could: possibility

points.name: Needn't and don't need to
points.can_do: Says that something is not necessary and separates it from a prohibition: You needn't wait. You don't need to come.
points.typical_errors: *You needn't to wait; You don't need come; You needn't park here* for a prohibition
points.sources: Murphy 32 · TE B1+: Needn't, don't need to, didn't need to, needn't have · EGP: B2 need: negative; needn't: lack of obligation

points.name: Didn't need to or needn't have
points.can_do: Separates an action that was not necessary and probably not done (didn't need to) from one that was done for nothing (needn't have done).
points.typical_errors: *We needn't hurried; We needn't have to hurry; We didn't need hurry*
points.sources: Murphy 32 · TE B1+: Needn't, don't need to, didn't need to, needn't have · EGP: C1 needn't have + -ed · Level: the list teaches it at B1+; EGP records needn't have only at C1

points.name: Should have, could have done: criticism and regret
points.can_do: Says that the right thing was not done or that a chance was missed: You should have told me. We could have won.
points.typical_errors: *You should told me; You should have tell me; You should had told me; You must have told me* as criticism
points.sources: Murphy 27, 33 · TE no line of its own (B1+: Past modals of deduction; B2: Modals, from memory) · EGP: B1 should: past affirmative, past negative, regret; B2 could: regret · In the app only inside the passive (should have been closed)

points.name: Deduction about the past: must have, might have, can't have done
points.can_do: Guesses about the past with the right certainty: She must have left. He might have forgotten. They can't have seen us.
points.typical_errors: *She must left; He must had left; She mustn't have seen us* for *can't have*; *He can have forgotten*
points.sources: Murphy 27, 28, 29 · TE B1+: Past modals of deduction; B2: Speculation and deduction · EGP: B2 must: past affirmative; could: past speculation; B1 might: past affirmative; C1 can: past negative deductions · Level: the B1+ list covers B1.2-B2.1; EGP mostly B2, so the second half

points.name: Be supposed to, be meant to
points.can_do: Talks about what is expected or arranged, and what people say: You're supposed to wear a helmet. It's supposed to be a great film.
points.typical_errors: *You are suppose to wear; You supposed to; It supposes to be*
points.sources: Murphy 45 · TE B2: Modals: permission, obligation, prohibition, necessity · EGP: B1 be supposed to: past expectation; B2 obligation, hearsay; be meant to

points.name: Modals with continuous forms: must be joking, might be working
points.can_do: Speculates about something in progress now or then: He must be working late. She might have been driving.
points.typical_errors: *He must working; She must be work; He might been sleeping*
points.sources: Murphy 28, 29 · TE B2: Speculation and deduction · EGP: B2 should be + -ing

points.name: Present simple passive: is / are + third form
points.can_do: Says what is done when the doer is unknown or not important: English is spoken here. These phones are made in China.
points.typical_errors: *English is speak here; These phones make in China; The windows is cleaned*
points.sources: Murphy 42 · TE A2: Present and past simple passive · EGP: A2 present simple, affirmative

points.name: Past simple passive: was / were + third form
points.can_do: Tells what was done in the past: The bridge was built in 1890. I was born in Riga.
points.typical_errors: *I am born in 1990; The bridge was build; The windows was broken; I born in*
points.sources: Murphy 42 · TE A2: Present and past simple passive · EGP: A2 past simple, affirmative

points.name: The doer with by, only when it matters
points.can_do: Adds by + the doer when it is new or important and leaves it out when it is not: This picture was painted by my grandfather.
points.typical_errors: *It was painted from my grandfather; My bike was stolen by somebody*
points.sources: Murphy 42 · TE A2: Present and past simple passive · EGP: A2 with by to add information; B1 giving focus with by

points.name: Passive negatives and questions
points.can_do: Makes passive negatives and questions by moving be: Where are these phones made? When was the castle built? It wasn't finished.
points.typical_errors: *Where these phones are made? When the castle was built? Did the castle was built?*
points.sources: Murphy 42 · TE A2: Present and past simple passive; B1: Passive verb forms · EGP: B1 present simple, negative; B2 past simple negative · The app has these tasks from A2.2

points.name: Active or passive?
points.can_do: Decides by asking who does the action, turns an active sentence into a passive one and back, and knows that verbs without an object have no passive.
points.typical_errors: *The accident was happened; My bike stole yesterday; The film was appeared in 2019*
points.sources: Murphy 42, 44 · TE B1: Active and passive · EGP: B1 present simple, past simple passive (increasing range)

points.name: Present continuous passive: is being done
points.can_do: Says that something is being done now or around now: The road is being repaired.
points.typical_errors: *The road is repairing; Your order is been prepared; The rooms is being cleaned*
points.sources: Murphy 43 · TE B1: Passive verb forms · EGP: B1 present continuous, affirmative

points.name: Present perfect passive: has been done
points.can_do: Gives news or a result without the doer: The email has been sent. Has the problem been solved yet?
points.typical_errors: *The email has sent; The problem have been solved; The tickets have been sold yesterday; has being fixed*
points.sources: Murphy 43 · TE B1: Passive verb forms · EGP: B2 present perfect simple, affirmative · Level: test-english B1, EGP B2

points.name: Future passive: will be done, is going to be done
points.can_do: Says what will be done: The results will be announced on Friday.
points.typical_errors: *The results will announced; You will be tell; Will be the meeting held online?*
points.sources: Murphy 43 · TE B1: Passive verb forms · EGP: B2 passive with will, future reference; B1 passive infinitive after going to · Level: test-english B1, EGP B2

points.name: Passive after modal verbs: must be done, can be bought
points.can_do: Uses modal + be + third form for rules, advice and possibility: Tickets can be bought online.
points.typical_errors: *The report must finished; Tickets can be buy; It must to be done; The door should be lock*
points.sources: Murphy 43 · TE B1: Passive verb forms; B1+: Passive: all tenses · EGP: B2 passive with modal verbs · Level: test-english B1, EGP B2

points.name: Passive after a past modal: should have been done
points.can_do: Criticises or guesses about the past in the passive: The window should have been closed. It must have been stolen.
points.typical_errors: *It should have closed; It should been closed; It must have being stolen*
points.sources: Murphy 43 · TE B1+: Passive: all tenses (from memory) · EGP: B2 passive: modal perfect · On the passive_modals card (B1.1-B1.2 in the app)

points.name: Passive in other tenses: was being done, had been done
points.can_do: Uses the passive in the past continuous and past perfect: The room was being cleaned. The car had been stolen before.
points.typical_errors: *The room was cleaning; The car had stolen; was been cleaned*
points.sources: Murphy 43 · TE B1+: Passive: all tenses · EGP: B2 past continuous affirmative; past perfect simple, affirmative

points.name: Passive infinitive and -ing: to be told, being asked
points.can_do: Uses the passive after verbs and prepositions: I want to be told. Nobody likes being criticised.
points.typical_errors: *I want to told; Nobody likes be criticised; I don't like to being asked*
points.sources: Murphy 43, 44 · TE B1+: Passive: all tenses (from memory) · EGP: B1-B2 passive infinitive; C1 non-finite clauses

points.name: Passive of verbs with two objects: I was given a book
points.can_do: Starts the passive with the person: I was given a ticket. She was offered the job.
points.typical_errors: *It was given me a ticket; To me was given; I was explained the rules*
points.sources: Murphy 44 · TE B2: Passive verbs with two objects · EGP: B1-B2 passive with verbs taking two objects

points.name: Passive with reporting verbs: It is said that … / He is said to …
points.can_do: Reports what people say or believe without naming them, with both patterns: It is said that the firm is in trouble. The firm is said to be in trouble.
points.typical_errors: *He is said that he is rich; It is said him to be rich; He is said to being*
points.sources: Murphy 45 · TE B1+: Passive with reporting verbs · EGP: B2 passive: summaries and evaluations; C1 summarising with it

points.name: Distancing: seem, appear, apparently, is believed to have done
points.can_do: Reports information without taking responsibility for it: He appears to have left. There is thought to be a problem.
points.typical_errors: *He seems that he left; It seems him to be; He is believed to left*
points.sources: Murphy 45 · TE B2: Distancing and passive of reporting verbs · EGP: B2 be supposed to: hearsay; C1 it + passive, summarising

points.name: Have something done
points.can_do: Says that somebody else does a service for us, in any tense: I had my hair cut. She's having her car repaired.
points.typical_errors: *I cut my hair at the hairdresser's; I had cleaned my car* (= I cleaned it); *She is having her car repair*
points.sources: Murphy 46 · TE B1+: Have something done · EGP: B2 have + object + -ed · Level: test-english B1+, EGP B2; the app starts at B1.1

points.name: Get something done; something bad that happened: had my bag stolen
points.can_do: Uses get as the informal form and have for an unpleasant experience: We got the windows cleaned. She had her bag stolen.
points.typical_errors: *She was stolen her bag; We got cleaned the windows*
points.sources: Murphy 46 · TE B1+: Have something done; B2: Get · EGP: C1 get + object + -ed; B2 have + object + -ed

points.name: Zero conditional: if + present, present
points.can_do: Talks about what always happens, and gives an instruction for a situation: If you heat ice, it melts. If you feel sick, stay at home.
points.typical_errors: TIME-CLAUSE: *If you will heat ice, it melts*; 3S: *If water boil, it turns*
points.sources: TE A2: First conditional and future time clauses; B1+: Zero and first conditional, future time clauses · EGP: A2 if + present simple; if clause + imperative · Not a Murphy EGiU unit (if + present is in units 25 and 38)

points.name: First conditional: if + present, will
points.can_do: Talks about a real possibility in the future and its result; either part can come first: If it rains, we'll stay at home.
points.typical_errors: TIME-CLAUSE: *If it will rain, we'll stay at home*; 3S: *If she call, I'll tell you*
points.sources: Murphy 25, 38 · TE A2: First conditional and future time clauses · EGP: B1 present simple if clause + will; A2 will after if

points.name: If or when
points.can_do: Uses if for something that may happen and when for something that will: If I see her, I'll tell her. When I see her, I'll tell her.
points.typical_errors: *When it rains tomorrow, we'll stay at home* for an uncertain event; *If I am older, I'll…*
points.sources: Murphy 25 · TE B1: First conditional, future time clauses · EGP: A2-B1 (not a separate EGP entry)

points.name: Unless = if … not
points.can_do: Replaces if … not with unless and keeps the verb positive: Unless you hurry, you'll miss the bus.
points.typical_errors: *Unless you don't hurry; Unless you will hurry*
points.sources: Murphy 115 · TE B1: First conditional, future time clauses; B2: Unless, even if, provided, as long as · EGP: B1 unless, exceptions

points.name: First conditional with may, might, can, should or an order in the result
points.can_do: Varies the result: If you finish early, you can go. If it rains, we might stay in.
points.typical_errors: *If you will finish early, you can go; If it rains, we might to stay*
points.sources: Murphy 38 · TE B1: First conditional, future time clauses · EGP: B1 present simple if clause + modal

points.name: Zero or first conditional: always, or this one time?
points.can_do: Chooses the present for what is always true and will for one future situation: If I drink coffee late, I can't sleep. If I drink this coffee, I won't sleep tonight.
points.typical_errors: *If it rains tomorrow, we stay at home*
points.sources: TE B1+: Zero and first conditional, future time clauses · EGP: A2-B1 · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Second conditional: if + past, would
points.can_do: Imagines something that is not true now or is unlikely: If I lived by the sea, I'd swim every day. What would you do if…?
points.typical_errors: IF-WOULD: *If I would have more money, I'd buy a car; If she knew, she will tell us*
points.sources: Murphy 38, 39 · TE A2: Second conditional; B1: Second conditional · EGP: B1 if + past simple + would, imagined situation · Level: test-english A2 and again B1, EGP B1; the app starts at B1.1. Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B1; the A2.2 path step is not needed.

points.name: If I were you, I'd …
points.can_do: Gives advice with If I were you and uses were for every person in careful English.
points.typical_errors: *If I am you, I'd call her; If I would be you; If I was you, I will*
points.sources: Murphy 39 · TE B1: Second conditional · EGP: B1 if I were you + would

points.name: First or second conditional: real or imagined?
points.can_do: Chooses by how real the situation is: If it rains, I'll stay at home. If I had wings, I'd fly.
points.typical_errors: *If I win the lottery, I'll buy a house* said without a ticket; *If I had time tomorrow, I will help* (mixing the two)
points.sources: Murphy 38 · TE B1: First and second conditionals · EGP: B1

points.name: Third conditional: if + had done, would have done
points.can_do: Imagines a different past and its result: If I had known, I would have called.
points.typical_errors: IF-WOULD: *If I would have known, I would have called; If I had known, I would have call; If we had took a taxi*
points.sources: Murphy 40 · TE B1: Third conditional · EGP: B1 if + past perfect + would have + -ed

points.name: Third conditional with could have, might have
points.can_do: Makes the imagined result less sure or about ability: If you had told me, I could have helped.
points.typical_errors: *If you told me, I could have helped; If you had told me, I could helped*
points.sources: Murphy 40 · TE B1+: Second and third conditionals (from memory) · EGP: C1 if + past perfect + modal verbs

points.name: Second or third conditional: now or then?
points.can_do: Chooses by time: If I had time, I'd help (now). If I'd had time, I'd have helped (then); reads 'd as had or would.
points.typical_errors: *If I had time yesterday, I would help; If I'd have known*
points.sources: Murphy 39, 40 · TE B1+: Second and third conditionals · EGP: B1 (both forms)

points.name: Mixed conditional: past condition, present result
points.can_do: Links a different past with a result now: If I had taken that job, I would be rich now.
points.typical_errors: *If I would have taken the job, I would be rich now; If he had studied medicine, he will be a doctor now*
points.sources: TE B2: Mixed conditionals · EGP: C1 if + past perfect + modal verbs, imagined situation (the nearest EGP entry) · Not in Murphy EGiU (units 38-40 treat the two times separately) Level: test-english B2, EGP C1

points.name: Mixed conditional: present condition, past result
points.can_do: Links a lasting fact with a result in the past: If he were more confident, he would have asked for a pay rise.
points.typical_errors: *If she is more patient, she wouldn't have shouted; If he was more confident, he would ask* about a past chance
points.sources: TE B2: Mixed conditionals · EGP: not a separate EGP entry · Not in Murphy EGiU

points.name: As long as, provided (that), even if, supposing
points.can_do: Uses other words than if for a condition: You can borrow it as long as you bring it back. Even if it rains, we'll go.
points.typical_errors: *As long as you will bring it back; Provided you would pay; Even it rains*
points.sources: Murphy 115 · TE B2: Unless, even if, provided, as long as · EGP: B2 conditions with as long as, provided

points.name: Inverted conditionals: Had I known …, Should you need …, Were she …
points.can_do: Recognises and forms the formal conditional without if: Should you have any questions, please contact us. Had I known, I would have helped.
points.typical_errors: *If had I known; Had I knew; Hadn't she missed the train* for *Had she not missed; Would you need help, call me*
points.sources: TE B2: All conditionals, alternatives to if, inversion · EGP: C1 inverted conditional with should; C2 inverted past perfect; C2 inverted were + to-infinitive · Not in Murphy EGiU; Hewings, Advanced Grammar in Use (from memory, not checked) Level: test-english B2, EGP C1-C2. Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B2.2 is recognising the form and making it when the start is given; choosing and transforming is C1 (x_inv_cond).

points.name: I wish / if only + past: a wish about now
points.can_do: Says that somebody would like the present to be different: I wish I had more time. If only I could drive.
points.typical_errors: *I wish I have more time; I wish I would have more time; I wish I can drive*
points.sources: Murphy 39, 41 · TE B1+: I wish / if only · EGP: B1 past simple with wish: regret that things are not different · The app has it at B2.2 only Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B1.2, as in the list; B1.2 tasks are to be written.

points.name: I wish / if only + had done: regret about the past
points.can_do: Regrets something that happened or did not happen: I wish I had studied harder. If only we had tested the app!
points.typical_errors: *I wish I studied harder* about a finished chance; *I wish I would have studied; I wish I have studied*
points.sources: Murphy 40, 41 · TE B1+: I wish / if only; B2: Wish, rather, if only, it's time · EGP: B2 past perfect after if only and wish, imagined past

points.name: I wish … would: wanting somebody or something to change
points.can_do: Complains about a habit or asks for a change: I wish you would listen. I wish it would stop raining.
points.typical_errors: *I wish I would have more time* (the same subject); *I wish you will listen; I wish you listen*
points.sources: Murphy 41 · TE B2: Wish, rather, if only, it's time · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: It's time to go; it's time for a break
points.can_do: Says that the moment for something has come: It's time to leave. It's time for lunch.
points.typical_errors: *It's time go; It's time for go; It's time that we go*
points.sources: Murphy 35 · TE B1: Had better, it's time · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: It's (high / about) time + subject + past
points.can_do: Says that something should already be happening: It's high time we went. It's about time you called your mother.
points.typical_errors: *It's high time we go; It's time we will go; It's high time to we went*
points.sources: Murphy 35 · TE B2: Wish, rather, if only, it's time · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: Would rather, would sooner, would prefer: what I prefer to do
points.can_do: States a preference: I'd rather walk. I'd rather not go. I'd prefer to stay. I'd rather walk than drive.
points.typical_errors: *I'd rather to walk; I'd rather walking; I'd prefer stay; I'd rather don't go; I would rather walk that drive*
points.sources: Murphy 59 · TE B1: Would rather, would sooner; B1+: Would rather, would prefer · EGP: B1 would prefer + to (would rather not found in EGP) · The app has it at B2.2 only Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B1.2, as in the list; B1.2 tasks are to be written.

points.name: I'd rather you + past: what I want somebody else to do
points.can_do: Asks politely for different behaviour: I'd rather you came a bit earlier. I'd rather you didn't call after ten.
points.typical_errors: *I'd rather you come earlier; I'd rather you to come; I'd rather you don't call*
points.sources: Murphy 59 · TE B2: Wish, rather, if only, it's time · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: Say or tell
points.can_do: Uses tell with a person and say without one: He told me (that) … / He said (that) … / He said to me …
points.typical_errors: SAY-TELL: *He said me that; She told that she was busy; He said, that he was tired*
points.sources: Murphy 48 · TE A2: Reported speech · EGP: A2 reported statements with say, with tell (pronoun shift, no tense shift) · Level: list A2 and EGP A2 for say / tell without a tense change; the app has its tasks from B1.1.

points.name: Reported statements: the tense goes one step back
points.can_do: Reports what somebody said after said / told: am → was, work → worked, will → would, can → could.
points.typical_errors: BACKSHIFT: *She said she is tired* (no longer true); *He said he will come; She said she can help*
points.sources: Murphy 47 · TE A2: Reported speech; B1: Reported speech · EGP: B1 reported statements, pronoun and tense shift · Level: test-english A2 and again B1; EGP A2 for say / tell with pronoun change, B1 for the tense change. Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B1 for the tense change (say / tell alone is A2.2); the A2.2 path step is not needed.

points.name: Reported speech: pronouns, time and place words
points.can_do: Changes I → he / she, my → his / her, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.
points.typical_errors: *She said I was tired* (for she); *He said he would come tomorrow* reported a week later
points.sources: Murphy 47, 48 · TE B1: Reported speech · EGP: B1 temporal shifts, future; B2 temporal shifts, past

points.name: Reported statements: past → past perfect, present perfect → past perfect
points.can_do: Reports a past or perfect tense: 'I lost my keys' → He said he had lost his keys. 'I've finished' → She said she had finished.
points.typical_errors: *He said he lost his keys* where the order matters; *She said she has finished; He said he had went*
points.sources: Murphy 47, 48 · TE B1: Reported speech · EGP: B2 past perfect: reports of statements

points.name: When the tense can stay: still true, says, has said
points.can_do: Knows that after a present reporting verb nothing changes, and that a fact that is still true may keep its tense: She says she's tired. He said the Earth goes round the Sun.
points.typical_errors: *She says she was tired* for a present state; in our tasks the step back is the form practised (teacher, 11 November)
points.sources: Murphy 48 · TE B1: Reported speech (from memory) · EGP: B2 citation, present simple

points.name: Reported requests and orders: told / asked somebody (not) to
points.can_do: Reports an order or a request with to + verb: He told me to wait. She asked me not to call.
points.typical_errors: *He told me wait; She asked me don't call; He said me to wait; She told to me to wait*
points.sources: Murphy 48 · TE A2: Reported speech; B1: Reported speech · EGP: B1 reported requests and commands; B2 negative

points.name: Reported wh-questions: He asked where I lived
points.can_do: Reports a question with a question word: statement word order, no do / did, tense one step back.
points.typical_errors: Q-ORDER: *He asked where did I live; She asked what was my name; He asked me where do I work*
points.sources: Murphy 50 · TE B1: Reported speech · EGP: B1 reported wh- questions

points.name: Reported yes / no questions: She asked if / whether …
points.can_do: Reports a yes / no question with if or whether and statement order: She asked if I liked coffee.
points.typical_errors: IND-YESNO: *She asked do I like coffee; He asked me that I was ready; She asked if did I like*
points.sources: Murphy 50 · TE B1: Reported speech · EGP: B1 reported yes-no questions

points.name: Reporting verbs + to: offer, refuse, promise, agree, threaten
points.can_do: Reports the meaning, not the words: 'Shall I help?' → She offered to help.
points.typical_errors: *She offered helping; He refused that he would pay; She promised me to come*
points.sources: Murphy 54 · TE B1+: Reporting verbs · EGP: B2 reporting verbs (increasing range) · The app has the whole topic at B2.2

points.name: Reporting verbs + person + to: advise, warn, remind, invite, encourage, persuade
points.can_do: 'Don't forget to call.' → She reminded me to call. 'You should rest.' → He advised me to rest.
points.typical_errors: *He advised to rest; She reminded to me to call; He warned me to not touch; She suggested me to go*
points.sources: Murphy 55 · TE B1+: Reporting verbs · EGP: B1 verbs + direct object + to-infinitive

points.name: Reporting verbs + -ing: suggest, admit, deny, recommend
points.can_do: 'Let's take a taxi.' → He suggested taking a taxi. 'I didn't take it.' → He denied taking it.
points.typical_errors: PATTERN: *He suggested me to take a taxi; He suggested to take; She denied to take it; He admitted to took*
points.sources: Murphy 53 · TE B1+: Reporting verbs · EGP: B2 verb + -ing form

points.name: Reporting verbs + preposition + -ing: apologise for, insist on, accuse of, congratulate on
points.can_do: 'I'm sorry I'm late.' → He apologised for being late. 'You cheated.' → They accused him of cheating.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *She insisted to pay; They accused him for cheating; He apologised to be late; congratulated me for passing*
points.sources: Murphy 62 · TE B1+: Reporting verbs · EGP: B2 (verb + preposition + -ing, not a separate EGP entry)

points.name: Yes / no questions and short answers: be, do, have, can
points.can_do: Starts the question with the right helping verb and answers with it: Are you tired? Do you work here? Can you swim? Yes, I do.
points.typical_errors: DO: *Are you like coffee? Do you tired? You like coffee?*; short answers *Yes, I like; Yes, I'm*
points.sources: Murphy 49 · TE A1: Questions: word order and question words · EGP: A1 yes / no with modal verbs; A2 with be, do, have

points.name: Wh-questions: question word + helping verb + subject
points.can_do: Asks with what, where, when, who, why, how, how much / many and keeps the order: Where do you live? What are you doing?
points.typical_errors: DO: *Where you live? What you are doing? Why she is late? How long you have been here?*
points.sources: Murphy 49 · TE A1: Questions: word order and question words; A2: Question forms · EGP: A2 wh- with auxiliary do, be, have, modal verbs

points.name: Choosing the helping verb across tenses: do, did, be, have
points.can_do: Picks be for -ing and adjectives, do / does / did for the simple tenses and have for the third form, in questions and negatives.
points.typical_errors: *Did you seen it? Do she work here? Are you work? Have you see?*
points.sources: Murphy 49, 51 · TE A2: Auxiliary verbs do, be, have · EGP: A2 auxiliary verbs have and do

points.name: So am I, neither do I
points.can_do: Agrees with a positive or a negative sentence using the same helping verb, and with too / either: A: I'm tired. B: So am I. / Me too. A: I don't smoke. B: Neither do I. / I don't either.
points.typical_errors: *So I am; So do I* after *I'm tired; Neither I do; Me too* after a negative; *Neither don't I*
points.sources: Murphy 51 · TE A2: So am I, neither do I · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: Subject questions: Who called? What happened?
points.can_do: Asks about the doer without do / does / did and about the object with it: Who called you? Who did you call?
points.typical_errors: DO: *What did happened? Who does live here? Who did call you?*; *What you want?*
points.sources: Murphy 49 · TE A2: Subject questions, questions with a preposition · EGP: A2 wh- questions (subject questions not a separate EGP entry)

points.name: Which / What / How many + noun as the subject
points.can_do: Asks without do when the question phrase is the subject: Which bus goes to the centre? How many people came?
points.typical_errors: *Which bus does go to the centre? How many people did come?*
points.sources: Murphy 49 · TE B1+: Questions: different types (from memory) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry · Level: taught with subject questions; the list line is from memory.

points.name: Questions with a preposition at the end
points.can_do: Leaves the preposition after the verb: Who are you talking to? What are you looking at? Where are you from?
points.typical_errors: *To who are you talking? About what are you thinking? Who are you waiting?*
points.sources: Murphy 49 · TE A2: Subject questions, questions with a preposition · EGP: A2 preposition stranding

points.name: Negative questions: Don't you …? Why didn't you …?
points.can_do: Shows surprise, checks or suggests with a negative question, and answers about the fact: Don't you like it? Why don't we go?
points.typical_errors: *Why you didn't call? Do not you like it?*; answering *Yes* to mean agreement with the negative
points.sources: Murphy 49 · TE B1+: Questions: different types · EGP: B1 negative questions with be, auxiliary verbs, modal verbs

points.name: Question tags: isn't it? don't you? did she?
points.can_do: Adds a tag with the opposite sign and the right helping verb and pronoun: You like tea, don't you? She isn't here, is she?
points.typical_errors: *You like tea, isn't it? She isn't here, isn't she? He went home, doesn't he?*
points.sources: Murphy 52 · TE B1: Question tags · EGP: A2 question tags (limited); B1 affirmative + negative, negative + affirmative · The app has tasks from A2.2

points.name: Special tags: aren't I? shall we? will you? nobody … they
points.can_do: Uses the tags that do not follow the simple rule: I'm late, aren't I? Let's go, shall we? Nobody called, did they?
points.typical_errors: *I'm late, amn't I? Let's go, will we? Nobody called, didn't he? Nothing happened, didn't it?*
points.sources: Murphy 52 · TE B1: Question tags · EGP: B2 tags with imperatives; C1 tags with there + be

points.name: Auxiliaries: emphasis, echo questions, avoiding repetition
points.can_do: Uses the helping verb alone: I do like it! A: I've lost my keys. B: Have you? I think so. I hope not.
points.typical_errors: *I think yes; I hope no; A: I've lost my keys. B: Did you?; I do liked it*
points.sources: Murphy 51 · TE B1+: Auxiliary verbs: different uses · EGP: B1 imperative do, emphasis; C1 past simple: emphasis with did

points.name: Indirect questions with a question word: Could you tell me where … is?
points.can_do: Asks politely with statement word order and no do: Could you tell me where the station is? Do you know what time the shop opens?
points.typical_errors: Q-ORDER: *Could you tell me where is the station? Do you know what time does the shop open?*
points.sources: Murphy 50 · TE B1+: Indirect questions · EGP: A2 indirect questions with Do you know + how / where / why / what · Level: test-english B1+, EGP A2; the app starts at B1.1

points.name: Indirect yes / no questions: Do you know if …?
points.can_do: Uses if or whether for a yes / no question inside another: Do you know if she is at home? I wonder whether it's open.
points.typical_errors: IND-YESNO: *Do you know is she at home? Can you tell me do you live here? I wonder does she know*
points.sources: Murphy 50 · TE B1+: Indirect questions · EGP: B1 wonder, reported thought

points.name: Question word + to: I don't know what to do
points.can_do: Shortens a question about what somebody should do: I don't know what to do. Can you show me how to use it?
points.typical_errors: Q-ORDER: *I don't know what should I do; I don't know what do; Show me how use it*
points.sources: Murphy 54 · TE no line of its own (A2: Infinitives and gerunds; B1: Gerund or infinitive) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry · The app has it at B2.2 only

points.name: Whether: after prepositions, with to, with or not
points.can_do: Uses whether, not if, after a preposition, before to + verb and with or not: It depends on whether the budget is approved. I can't decide whether to accept.
points.typical_errors: *It depends on if; I can't decide if to accept; It depends whether or no*
points.sources: Murphy 50 · TE B1+: Indirect questions (from memory) · EGP: C2 whether or not, formal

points.name: A question clause as the subject: Why the system failed remains unclear
points.can_do: Starts a formal sentence with an embedded question and keeps statement order in it: How the funds were spent is not known. Whether he will come is unclear.
points.typical_errors: *Why did the system fail remains unclear; If he will come is unclear*
points.sources: TE no line in the lists · EGP: C1 what cleft clause as subject (the nearest EGP entry) · Not in Murphy EGiU; no line in the lists (the app teaches it at B2.2)

points.name: Whatever, whoever, whenever, wherever, however
points.can_do: Says 'it does not matter what / who / when': Whatever you decide, I'll help. Come whenever you like. Whoever arrives last washes up.
points.typical_errors: *Whomever arrives last; Whatever you will decide; Whatever do you decide*
points.sources: TE B1+: Whatever, whenever… · EGP: C1 whatever, wherever, however as subordinating conjunctions · Not a Murphy EGiU unit Level: test-english B1+, EGP C1

points.name: Like, love, hate + -ing; want + to
points.can_do: Follows the verbs of liking with -ing and want with to: I like cooking. I want to go.
points.typical_errors: PATTERN: *I like cook; I want go; I want going*
points.sources: Murphy 53, 58 · TE A1: Verb + to + infinitive, verb + -ing · EGP: A1 verb + to-infinitive; like + to-infinitive or -ing; A2 enjoy + -ing · The app starts the topic at A2.2

points.name: Verb + to: want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, promise
points.can_do: Uses to + base form after these verbs, with not before to in the negative: He decided to stay. She promised not to tell.
points.typical_errors: PATTERN: *I want going home; He decided stay; She promised to not tell; I hope see you*
points.sources: Murphy 54 · TE A2: Infinitives and gerunds · EGP: A2 verbs + to-infinitive (limited range); B1 increasing range

points.name: Verb + -ing: enjoy, finish, mind, avoid, keep, suggest
points.can_do: Uses the -ing form after these verbs: I enjoy reading. Would you mind waiting?
points.typical_errors: PATTERN: *I enjoy to read; She finished to work; Do you mind to wait? He suggested to go*
points.sources: Murphy 53 · TE A2: Infinitives and gerunds · EGP: A2 enjoy + -ing; B1 verb + -ing form

points.name: -ing as the subject: Swimming is good for you
points.can_do: Starts a sentence with an activity: Learning a language takes time. Smoking is not allowed.
points.typical_errors: *Learn a language takes time; To smoking is not allowed; Swim is good*
points.sources: TE A2: Infinitives and gerunds (from memory) · EGP: A2 -ing forms as object; B2 -ing forms as subject · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Go + -ing, go to, go for: go shopping, go for a walk
points.can_do: Uses the fixed patterns with go for activities: go swimming, go to the gym, go for a run, go on holiday.
points.typical_errors: *go to shopping; go for swimming; go to home*
points.sources: TE A2: Go · EGP: not found in EGP · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Adjective + to: It's easy to …, I'm glad to …
points.can_do: Uses to + base form after adjectives: It's difficult to understand him. I was sorry to hear that. It's too cold to swim.
points.typical_errors: *It's easy understand; It's difficult for understand; I'm glad seeing you*
points.sources: Murphy 65 · TE A2: Infinitives and gerunds (from memory) · EGP: B1 it + be + adjective + infinitive; too + to-infinitive · Level: EGP B1; the A2 list line is from memory.

points.name: Preposition + -ing: interested in learning, before leaving
points.can_do: Uses -ing after every preposition: I'm good at cooking. Thank you for helping. She left without saying goodbye.
points.typical_errors: PATTERN: *interested in learn; before to leave; without say; thank you for help; instead of to talk*
points.sources: Murphy 60 · TE B1: Gerund or infinitive · EGP: A2 preposition + -ing

points.name: Verb + person + to: I want you to come
points.can_do: Says what one person wants, asks or tells another to do: I want you to come. She asked me to help. They told us not to wait.
points.typical_errors: PATTERN: *I want that you come; She asked me help; He told to me to wait; I'd like you coming*
points.sources: Murphy 55 · TE B2: Verb + object + infinitive / gerund (first met in A2-B1: Reported speech) · EGP: B1 verbs + direct object + to-infinitive

points.name: Make and let + person + base form
points.can_do: Uses the base form without to: She made me laugh. Let me help. My parents didn't let me go.
points.typical_errors: *She made me to laugh; Let me to help; They didn't let me going*
points.sources: Murphy 55 · TE B2: Verb + object + infinitive / gerund · EGP: B1 make, let + infinitive without to

points.name: Verbs with both forms and the same meaning: start, begin, continue, like
points.can_do: Knows that both forms are right after these verbs and that would like takes only to.
points.typical_errors: *I like work with him* (base form); *I would like going*
points.sources: Murphy 56, 58 · TE B1: Gerund or infinitive · EGP: A2 verbs + to-infinitive or -ing

points.name: Stop, remember, forget, try, regret + -ing or to: a different meaning
points.can_do: Chooses the form by meaning: I stopped smoking / I stopped to smoke. Remember to call / I remember calling. Try to sleep / Try drinking tea.
points.typical_errors: *I stopped to smoke* meaning I quit; *Remember calling her* as a reminder; *I forgot locking the door* meaning I did not lock it
points.sources: Murphy 56, 57 · TE B1: Gerund or infinitive; B1+: Gerund or infinitive · EGP: B2 to-infinitive or -ing form, meaning · Level: test-english B1, EGP B2

points.name: To + -ing: look forward to, be used to, object to
points.can_do: Recognises to as a preposition: I look forward to seeing you. I'm used to driving on the left.
points.typical_errors: *I look forward to see you; I'm looking forward to hear from you; I object to pay*
points.sources: Murphy 60, 62 · TE B1: Gerund or infinitive (from memory) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: It's worth -ing, there's no point in -ing, it's no use -ing
points.can_do: Uses -ing after these expressions: It's worth trying. There's no point in waiting. I had difficulty finding it.
points.typical_errors: *It's worth to try; There's no point to wait; I had difficulty to find it*
points.sources: Murphy 63 · TE no line in the lists · EGP: not found in EGP · Standard point from Murphy unit 63; no content and no list line

points.name: Verb + person + -ing: I can't imagine him doing that
points.can_do: Puts a new subject before -ing: Do you mind me opening the window? I remember her saying so.
points.typical_errors: *Do you mind that I open; I can't imagine him to do that; I remember she saying*
points.sources: Murphy 53 · TE B2: Verb + object + infinitive / gerund · EGP: B2 verb + new subject + -ing form

points.name: See, hear, watch somebody do / doing
points.can_do: Uses the base form for the whole action and -ing for part of it: I saw him cross the road. I saw him crossing the road.
points.typical_errors: *I saw him to cross; I heard her sang; I saw him crossed*
points.sources: Murphy 67 · TE B2: Verbs of the senses (from memory) · EGP: B2 verbs of senses + object + -ing; C1 + infinitive

points.name: Complex gerunds and infinitives: having done, to have done, being told
points.can_do: Uses perfect and passive forms after verbs: He denied having seen it. She seems to have left. I hate being told what to do.
points.typical_errors: *He denied to have seen; She seems to left; He admitted have taken*
points.sources: Murphy 53, 54 · TE B2: Complex gerunds and infinitives · EGP: C1-C2 non-finite perfect clauses and complements

points.name: Reduced infinitives: I'd love to. I didn't mean to.
points.can_do: Stops at to instead of repeating the verb: A: Are you coming? B: I'd like to, but I can't.
points.typical_errors: *I'd like, but I can't; I didn't mean; Yes, I want*
points.sources: TE B2: Reduced infinitives · EGP: not a separate EGP entry (B2 used to: ellipsis) · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Verbs with two objects: give me a present / give a present to me
points.can_do: Uses both orders and chooses to or for: She sent her mother a letter. He bought a gift for his mother.
points.typical_errors: TWO-OBJ: *I bought a present to my sister; She gave to me a book; He sent to his mother a letter*
points.sources: TE A2: Verbs with two objects · EGP: B1 (verbs taking two objects, in the passive) · Not a Murphy EGiU unit (the passive side is unit 44)

points.name: Give it to me: a pronoun as the thing
points.can_do: Puts a pronoun thing first and adds to / for: Show it to me. I'll buy them for you.
points.typical_errors: *Give me it* (heard in informal British English; the tasks practise *Give it to me*); *Show me them; I'll buy you it*
points.sources: TE A2: Verbs with two objects · EGP: not a separate EGP entry · Not a Murphy EGiU unit Level: one step after the basic pattern of the A2 list.

points.name: Explain, describe, suggest, say: the thing first, then to + person
points.can_do: Never puts the person directly after these verbs: Can you explain the rules to me? He suggested a plan to us.
points.typical_errors: TWO-OBJ: *Can you explain me the problem? She said me the truth; Describe me the man; introduce my colleague for you*
points.sources: Murphy 132 · TE A2: Verbs with two objects (the exceptions) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry · Level: one step after the basic pattern of the A2 list.

points.name: Do or make
points.can_do: Uses the fixed combinations: do homework, do the dishes, do business; make a mistake, make a decision, make dinner.
points.typical_errors: *do a mistake; make homework; do a decision; make business*
points.sources: TE A2: Do vs make; B1+: Do or make · EGP: not in EGP (vocabulary) · Vocabulary, not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Get: get tired, get home, get a letter
points.can_do: Uses get for become (get cold), arrive (get home, get to work), receive and fetch.
points.typical_errors: *get to home; I got tired* confused with *I was tired; get in the bus*
points.sources: TE A2: Get · EGP: B1 get + -ed · Vocabulary, not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Get in grammar patterns: get married, get somebody to do, get something done
points.can_do: Uses get for the passive and for causing: They got married. I got him to help. Get your hair cut.
points.typical_errors: *I got him help; I got him helping* for persuading; *They got marry*
points.sources: Murphy 44, 46 · TE B2: Get · EGP: B1 get + -ed; B2 get + object + to-infinitive; C1 get + object + -ed

points.name: Phrasal verbs: get up, turn on, look for
points.can_do: Understands and uses the most common verb + particle combinations as single meanings.
points.typical_errors: *I stand up at seven* for *get up; put off the light; look the keys*
points.sources: Murphy 137 · TE A2: Phrasal verbs · EGP: A2 phrasal verbs: no object; verb + pronoun + particle

points.name: Phrasal verbs and the object: turn it off, look after her
points.can_do: Puts a pronoun between the verb and the particle when the verb can be separated and after the preposition when it cannot: Turn it off. Look after her. Also three-word verbs: I get on with her. We ran out of milk.
points.typical_errors: *Turn off it; Pick up me at six; Look her after*
points.sources: Murphy 137, 138, 139, 140, 141, 142, 143, 144, 145 · TE B1: Phrasal verbs 1-3 · EGP: B1 verb + pronoun + particle; verb + particle + object

points.name: Regular plurals: -s, -es, -ies
points.can_do: Forms and spells regular plurals: books, buses, cities, days.
points.typical_errors: *two bus; citys; dayes; a books*
points.sources: Murphy App. 6 · TE A1: A / an, plurals · EGP: A1 plural -s; A2 -es, -ies

points.name: Irregular plurals: children, people, men, women, teeth, feet
points.can_do: Uses the plurals that do not add -s, with a plural verb: The children are tired.
points.typical_errors: IRR-PLURAL: *childs, childrens, peoples, tooths, foots, mouses, womans*
points.sources: Murphy 79 · TE A1: A / an, plurals · EGP: A2 irregular plural nouns

points.name: Always plural: jeans, glasses, scissors; the police are
points.can_do: Uses a plural verb and some / a pair of with these nouns: My jeans are new. The police are here.
points.typical_errors: IRR-PLURAL: *The police is here; a jeans; My trousers is; a scissors*
points.sources: Murphy 79 · TE no line of its own (A1: A / an, plurals) · EGP: A2 nouns only used in the plural; B1 collective nouns

points.name: Subject and verb: my friend lives, my friends live
points.can_do: Makes the verb agree with a noun subject, also after and: My sister works. Tom and Anna live here. The shops are open.
points.typical_errors: 3S / AGREE: *My sister work; Tom and Anna lives here; The shops is open; My parents has*
points.sources: Murphy 2, 79 · TE A1: Present simple (no line of its own) · EGP: A1 present simple affirmative

points.name: The verb agrees with the main noun: one of my friends lives …
points.can_do: Finds the real subject in a longer phrase: One of my friends lives in Oslo. The people in this office are nice.
points.typical_errors: AGREE / PLURAL: *One of my friends live; one of the local bank; The people in this office is; a person who prefer*
points.sources: Murphy 79, 88 · TE no line in A2-B2 (returns in C1: Subject-verb agreement) · EGP: B1 superlative one of the · The app teaches it at A2.1-A2.2

points.name: Countable and uncountable: a / an, some, any
points.can_do: Knows which nouns can be counted and uses a / an with one, some in positive sentences, any in negatives and questions.
points.typical_errors: *a water; an advice; I have any friends; There aren't some eggs; a money*
points.sources: Murphy 69, 71, 85 · TE A1: A, some, any: countable and uncountable · EGP: A2 uncountable nouns; some and any · The app starts the topic at A2.2

points.name: Some in offers and requests; any = it does not matter which
points.can_do: Uses some in a question that offers or asks for something, and any in a positive sentence: Would you like some tea? Take any seat.
points.typical_errors: *Would you like any coffee?* as an offer; *Can I have any water?*
points.sources: Murphy 85 · TE B1: Much, many, a lot, little, few, some, any, no · EGP: A2 some as subject and object; B1 quantity determiners (increasing range)

points.name: Much, many, a lot of; How much? How many?
points.can_do: Chooses by countable or uncountable and by sentence type: How many people? Not much time. A lot of friends.
points.typical_errors: *How much people? many money; I have much time* (positive)
points.sources: Murphy 87 · TE A1: Much, many, a lot of, a little, a few · EGP: A2 much, many with negative; B1 interrogative

points.name: A few, a little
points.can_do: Says 'a small number' and 'a small amount': a few friends, a little time.
points.typical_errors: *a few money; a little friends; few of time*
points.sources: Murphy 87 · TE A1: Much, many, a lot of, a little, a few · EGP: A2 quantity with plural / uncountable nouns

points.name: Few and little without a: almost none
