points.can_do: Hears the negative meaning: I have few friends here (not enough) / I have a few friends (some).
points.typical_errors: *I have little friends; I have a few friends* meaning almost none
points.sources: Murphy 87 · TE B1: Much, many, a lot, little, few, some, any, no · EGP: B2 little / few · Level: the A2 list names little and few; the negative meaning without a is EGP B2, so it is placed with the B1 list line.

points.name: Too, too much, too many, enough
points.can_do: Says 'more than is good' and 'as much as is needed' and puts enough after an adjective and before a noun: too expensive, too many cars, big enough, enough chairs.
points.typical_errors: *too much expensive; enough big; too many traffic; very expensive* meaning too expensive
points.sources: Murphy 103 · TE A2: Too, too much, enough · EGP: A2 too with adjectives; B1 with enough; so much, too much

points.name: Too … to, … enough to
points.can_do: Adds what is impossible or possible: It's too cold to swim. She isn't old enough to drive. It's too heavy for me to carry.
points.typical_errors: *too cold for swim; It's too heavy that I carry; enough old to drive; too cold to swimming*
points.sources: Murphy 103 · TE A2: Too, too much, enough (from memory) · EGP: B1 too + to-infinitive; B2 enough + to-infinitive · Level: EGP B1-B2; the A2 list line is from memory.

points.name: No, none, not any
points.can_do: Uses no before a noun, none alone or with of, and only one negative: There's no milk = There isn't any milk. None of them came.
points.typical_errors: DOUBLE-NEG: *There isn't no milk; None people came; No of them; I don't have nothing*
points.sources: Murphy 86 · TE B1: Any, no, none · EGP: A2 determiner no; B2 none of + pronoun · On the quantity card only as a Watch out point

points.name: Most, most of, the most
points.can_do: Separates most people (in general), most of the people (a known group) and the most (superlative).
points.typical_errors: *Most of people; The most people think; most of my the friends*
points.sources: Murphy 88 · TE A2: Most, most of, the most · EGP: A2 determiner + of + determiner

points.name: All, both, either, neither (+ of)
points.can_do: Talks about two or more things: Both films are good. Neither of them is cheap. All (of) my friends came. Either day is fine.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *Both of films; Neither of them are* (formal: is); *All of people; The both; Neither didn't come*
points.sources: Murphy 88, 89 · TE B1: All, both; B1: Both, either, neither; B1+: All, most, both, either, neither, any, no, none · EGP: B1 both, a few as pronouns; C1 either, neither + of / with singular nouns

points.name: Each, every, all, whole
points.can_do: Uses a singular noun and verb after each and every, and separates all day from every day, all the book from the whole book.
points.typical_errors: AGREE / NP-ORDER: *Every students have; all the day; my all section; each of student*
points.sources: Murphy 90, 91 · TE B1+: All, most, both, either, neither, any, no, none (from memory) · EGP: B2 each as pronoun · On the agreement card (every + singular verb), A2 in the app

points.name: Another, other, others, the other
points.can_do: Chooses by number and by whether the thing is known: another coffee, other people, the other shoe, the others.
points.typical_errors: *another people; others students; the another one; other one*
points.sources: TE B1: Another, other, others · EGP: B1 another; the other · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Someone, anything, nobody, everywhere
points.can_do: Uses some- in positive sentences, any- in questions and negatives, no- with a positive verb, every- for all.
points.typical_errors: *I didn't see somebody; anybody didn't come*
points.sources: Murphy 85, 86 · TE A2: Something, anything, nothing · EGP: A2 indefinite pronouns as subject, object

points.name: One negative only: I didn't see anybody / I saw nobody
points.can_do: Avoids the double negative: I don't know anything. Nobody called.
points.typical_errors: DOUBLE-NEG: *I didn't see nobody; I don't know nothing; Nobody didn't call*
points.sources: Murphy 86 · TE A2: Something, anything, nothing; B1+: Double negatives · EGP: A2 negative + anything

points.name: Everybody is, nobody knows: singular verb, they / their
points.can_do: Uses a singular verb after these words and they / their to refer back: Everybody knows. Somebody left their bag.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *Everybody are here; Everyone know him; Nobody have*
points.sources: Murphy 86, 90 · TE A2: Something, anything, nothing · EGP: A2 indefinite pronouns as subject; B2 generic their

points.name: Something nice, anyone else, nothing to do
points.can_do: Puts the adjective, else or to + verb after the word: somewhere quiet, nothing interesting, something to drink.
points.typical_errors: NP-ORDER: *I have nice something; else somebody; nothing for do*
points.sources: TE B1: Any, no, none (from memory) · EGP: A2 with adjective; with else; with to-infinitive · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: A / an with a singular noun; jobs
points.can_do: Uses a or an by the first sound and never leaves a singular countable noun bare: a book, an hour, She is a nurse.
points.typical_errors: ARTICLE: *She is teacher; We have new colleague; a apple; an university*
points.sources: Murphy 71, 72 · TE A1: A / an, plurals · EGP: A1 articles with nouns; a + adjectives · The app starts the topic at A2.2

points.name: A or the: first mention, then known
points.can_do: Uses a for something new to the listener and the when both know which one: I saw a dog. The dog was huge.
points.typical_errors: ARTICLE / THE: *I saw dog; Can you open a window?* for the only window; *The dog* at first mention
points.sources: Murphy 72 · TE A1: A / an, the, no article · EGP: A1 articles with nouns

points.name: The: the sun, the same, the best, the first; play the piano
points.can_do: Uses the when there is only one, with superlatives and ordinals, the same, and with musical instruments.
points.typical_errors: THE: *Sun is hot today; She is best student; We live in same street; play piano*
points.sources: Murphy 72, 73 · TE A1: A / an, the, no article; B1: A(n), the, no article · EGP: A2 the + superlatives; the + adjectives, specifying · Level: the A1 list names the; these uses come half a level later, with the superlative already known. The app has their tasks at A2.2-B1.1.

points.name: No article for things in general: Life is short. I like coffee.
points.can_do: Leaves out the with plural and uncountable nouns in general and uses it for a particular one: Children love games / the children in my class.
points.typical_errors: THE: *The life is beautiful; I like the dogs* (in general); *He prefers an action instead of a talking*
points.sources: Murphy 75 · TE B1: A(n), the, no article · EGP: A1 no article; B2 uncountable nouns: no article

points.name: School or the school: places used for their purpose; meals; by bus
points.can_do: Leaves out the article in go to bed / school / work / hospital / prison, at home, have lunch, by car.
points.typical_errors: THE: *I go to the bed at eleven; She is at the work; have a lunch; by the bus; go to home*
points.sources: Murphy 74 · TE B1: A(n), the, no article · EGP: A1 preposition + no article; B1 preposition + no article

points.name: Names with and without the: Latvia, the Netherlands, the Daugava
points.can_do: Uses no article with most countries, cities, streets and lakes, and the with rivers, seas, oceans, plural names, republics and kingdoms.
points.typical_errors: THE: *He lives in the Latvia; I'm learning the Spanish; Daugava is long; in United States*
points.sources: Murphy 77, 78 · TE B1: A(n), the, no article · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: The + adjective: the rich, the elderly, the unemployed
points.can_do: Talks about a group of people with the + adjective and a plural verb: The elderly need more care.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *The elderly needs; the riches; the poors; riches have*
points.sources: Murphy 76 · TE B1+: Adjectives without a noun · EGP: B2 (not a separate EGP entry)

points.name: My, your, his, her, its, our, their; I, you, he, she
points.can_do: Uses the subject pronoun before the verb and the possessive word before the noun: She is my sister. Their car is new.
points.typical_errors: *He is me brother; she book; they car; it's colour* for *its*; *your* / *you're*
points.sources: TE A1: Possessive adjectives and subject pronouns · EGP: A1 possessive determiners with nouns; subject pronouns · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Object pronouns: me, him, her, us, them
points.can_do: Uses the object form after a verb or a preposition: Call me. I know them. This is for her.
points.typical_errors: *I know they; Call I; for she; I like he*
points.sources: TE A1: Object pronouns · EGP: A1 object pronouns · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Possessive 's and Whose …?
points.can_do: Shows who something belongs to: my sister's name, my parents' house; Whose bag is this?
points.typical_errors: POSSESSIVE: *My new colleague name is Marta; the name of my sister; Who's bag is this?; my parent's house* for two parents
points.sources: Murphy 81 · TE A1: Whose, possessive 's · EGP: A2 singular noun + 's; B1 irregular plural + 's; B2 plural noun + s'

points.name: Mine, yours, hers, ours, theirs; a friend of mine
points.can_do: Uses the possessive pronoun without a noun: This is mine. Is that yours? She's a friend of mine.
points.typical_errors: *This is my; It's the mine; a friend of me; hers book; your's*
points.sources: Murphy 83 · TE A2: Pronouns and possessives · EGP: A2 mine, yours; + of mine

points.name: Myself, yourself, themselves; by myself, on my own
points.can_do: Uses a reflexive pronoun when the subject and the object are the same, and by myself for alone: I cut myself. She lives by herself.
points.typical_errors: *I cut me; He hurt hisself; They enjoyed theirselves; I feel myself good; We met ourselves at six* for each other
points.sources: Murphy 82, 83 · TE B1: Reflexive pronouns · EGP: A2 same subject and object; B1 by + singular; after prepositions; for emphasis

points.name: Each other, one another; reflexive for emphasis; verbs without myself
points.can_do: Separates themselves from each other, adds emphasis (I did it myself) and leaves out the pronoun after feel, relax, concentrate, meet.
points.typical_errors: *They looked at themselves* for each other; *I feel myself tired; Relax yourself; We know us for years*
points.sources: Murphy 82 · TE B2: Reflexive and reciprocal pronouns · EGP: B1 each other; B2 one another; reflexive plural, for emphasis

points.name: Generic pronouns: you, one, we, they
points.can_do: Talks about people in general: You never know. One should be careful. They say it will snow.
points.typical_errors: *One never know; You never knows; It says that* for *They say*
points.sources: TE B2: Generic pronouns · EGP: A2 you, general; B1 one, general, formal; B2 we, us; gender-neutral they · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Uncountable in English: advice, information, furniture, news, luggage
points.can_do: Uses these nouns with no plural, no a / an and a singular verb: some advice, a piece of furniture, The news is good.
points.typical_errors: UNCOUNT: *The news are good; Your advices; an information; My hairs; furnitures; a luggage*
points.sources: Murphy 69, 70 · TE A2: Much, many, little, few, some, any (no line of its own) · EGP: A2 uncountable nouns; with determiners, quantity; containers, quantity expressions

points.name: Noun + noun, 's or of: a bus driver, my sister's car, the end of the film
points.can_do: Chooses the right way to join two nouns: noun + noun for a kind of thing, 's for people, of for things.
points.typical_errors: *a driver of bus; a car's door; my sister car; a ten-years-old boy*
points.sources: Murphy 80, 81 · TE B2: Compound nouns and possessives · EGP: B1 noun + of + possessive; B2 of + noun phrase 's

points.name: 's with time and distance: two hours' walk, yesterday's news
points.can_do: Uses the possessive with time expressions: a week's holiday, in three days' time, today's paper.
points.typical_errors: *two hours walk; a two hour's walk; yesterday news; three day's time*
points.sources: Murphy 81 · TE B2: Possessive 's with time (two hours' walk) · EGP: B2 plural noun + s'

points.name: Adjectives: before the noun, after be, no plural
points.can_do: Puts the adjective before the noun or after be and never adds -s to it: a big house, The houses are big.
points.typical_errors: *a house big; two smalls boxes; the news interesting; She is a girl tall*
points.sources: Murphy 99 · TE A1: Adjectives · EGP: A1 attributive, predicative with be · On the adj_order card as one form line

points.name: Adjective or adverb: quick / quickly, good / well
points.can_do: Uses an adjective for a noun and an adverb for a verb, with -ly spelling and the irregular well: a careful driver, She drives carefully.
points.typical_errors: *She speaks English very good; He drives careful; She sings beautiful; easyly, happyly*
points.sources: Murphy 100 · TE A1: Adverbs of manner or adjectives · EGP: A2 adverbs of manner, end position · The app starts the topic at A2.2

points.name: Fast, hard, late; hardly, lately
points.can_do: Uses fast, hard and late without -ly and knows that hardly means almost not and lately means recently.
points.typical_errors: *He drives fastly; She works hardly* meaning a lot; *I arrived lately*
points.sources: Murphy 101 · TE no line of its own (A1: Adverbs of manner or adjectives) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: Always, usually, often, sometimes, never: where they go
points.can_do: Puts the frequency word before the main verb and after be: She often walks. He is always late.
points.typical_errors: ADV-PLACE: *I go always by bus; She always is late; He never doesn't come; Always I get up at seven*
points.sources: Murphy 110 · TE A1: Adverbs of frequency · EGP: A1 frequency, mid position

points.name: Very, really, quite, too + adjective; I like it very much
points.can_do: Makes an adjective stronger or weaker and puts very much at the end: quite cold, really good, I like it very much.
points.typical_errors: *I very like it; I like very much it; too much cold; very much good*
points.sources: Murphy 104 · TE no line of its own (A1: Adjectives; A2: Too, too much, enough) · EGP: A1 very; A2 degree adverbs

points.name: Absolutely amazing, very good: strong and normal adjectives
points.can_do: Uses absolutely / completely with strong adjectives and very / extremely with normal ones: absolutely exhausted, very tired.
points.typical_errors: *very amazing; absolutely good; very exhausted; completely tired*
points.sources: TE B1+: Pretty, rather, quite, fairly (from memory) · EGP: C1 with extreme adverbs · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Quite, pretty, rather, fairly
points.can_do: Grades an opinion and places the word: quite a good film, a rather long day, pretty tired; quite right = completely.
points.typical_errors: *a quite good film; rather a bit; a pretty much; quite a tired*
points.sources: Murphy 104 · TE B1+: Pretty, rather, quite, fairly · EGP: B1 quite a; B2 rather a

points.name: Look, sound, feel, seem, taste + adjective
points.can_do: Uses an adjective, not an adverb, after these verbs: That sounds good. You look tired. I feel well / good.
points.typical_errors: *That sounds well; You look tiredly; It smells badly; She seems happily*
points.sources: Murphy 99, 101 · TE B1+: Verbs of the senses · EGP: A2 linking verbs + adjective · Level: list B1+, EGP A2; taught by the app from A2.2 on the adverbs card.

points.name: Look like + noun, look as if + clause
points.can_do: Separates the three patterns: You look tired. You look like your father. It looks as if it's going to rain.
points.typical_errors: *You look like tired; It looks like to rain; She looks as her mother; It sounds as a good idea*
points.sources: Murphy 118 · TE B1+: Verbs of the senses; B2: Verbs of the senses · EGP: B1 sense verbs + as if / as though; linking verb + like; B2 as if / as though + finite clause

points.name: Position of adverbs: verb + object, place before time, mid-position
points.can_do: Keeps the verb and its object together and puts place before time: I like coffee very much. We went to Rome last year. I've already seen it. She probably won't come.
points.typical_errors: ADV-PLACE: *I like very much coffee; We went last year to Rome; I have seen already it; She won't probably come*
points.sources: Murphy 109, 110 · TE B1+: Position of adverbs; A1: Basic word order · EGP: A2 adverbs: mid position, end position (manner, degree)

points.name: Bored or boring: -ed and -ing adjectives
points.can_do: Uses -ed for how a person feels and -ing for the thing or person that causes it: I'm bored. The film is boring.
points.typical_errors: ED-ING: *I am boring* (= I feel bored); *The lesson was very interested; It was a tired day; I'm very interesting in history*
points.sources: Murphy 98 · TE B1: -ed / -ing adjectives; B1+: -ed / -ing adjectives · EGP: not a separate EGP entry (C1 past participle as adjective) · The app starts at A2.2; the list has it at B1

points.name: Adjective order: a lovely old house, a big red car
points.can_do: Puts opinion before fact and facts in the usual order (size, age, shape, colour, origin, material), with at most two or three adjectives.
points.typical_errors: NP-ORDER: *an old lovely house; a red big car; a wooden nice new table*
points.sources: Murphy 99 · TE B1+: Adjective order · EGP: B1 combining adjectives before the noun; B2 complex noun phrases with adjectives · The app starts at B1.1

points.name: Compound adjectives with numbers: a five-star hotel, a ten-minute walk
points.can_do: Joins number and noun with a hyphen and keeps the noun singular: a two-hour film, a 20-year-old student.
points.typical_errors: *a five-stars hotel; a ten minutes walk; a 20-years-old student; a two hours film*
points.sources: Murphy 80 · TE B1: Compound adjectives with numbers · EGP: B1 compound adjectives

points.name: Compound adjectives: well-known, good-looking, part-time
points.can_do: Forms and understands adjectives made of two words: a well-paid job, a hard-working student, a last-minute change.
points.typical_errors: *a good-looked man; a hard-worked student; a well-pay job*
points.sources: TE B2: Compound adjectives · EGP: B2 compound adjectives (increasing range); C1 wide range · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Comparatives: -er, more … than; better, worse
points.can_do: Compares two things with the right form and spelling: bigger, easier, more expensive than, better, worse, further.
points.typical_errors: COMPARE: *more tall; more bigger; more better; older that me; gooder; expensiver*
points.sources: Murphy 105 · TE A1: Comparative adjectives · EGP: A2 comparatives: -er, with more, irregular, with than

points.name: Superlatives: the -est, the most …; the best, the worst
points.can_do: Compares one with all the others and adds in / of: the tallest in the class, the most expensive, the best.
points.typical_errors: COMPARE: *the most good; the most tallest; the tallest of the class; she is tallest; the more expensive of all*
points.sources: Murphy 108 · TE A1: Superlative adjectives · EGP: A2 superlatives: with -est, the most, with in / of + noun

points.name: As … as, not as … as; the same as, different from
points.can_do: Says that two things are equal or not: as fast as, not as heavy as, the same as mine, different from yours.
points.typical_errors: COMPARE: *as fast than; the same age like; not so heavy than; the same that; different than* (US) / *different of*
points.sources: Murphy 107 · TE A2: Comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs · EGP: B1 as … as; the same (+ noun) + as

points.name: Comparing adverbs: more slowly, faster, better, the most carefully
points.can_do: Compares how things are done: She drives more carefully than me. He runs faster. Who works the hardest?
points.typical_errors: *more fast; more quicklier; he speaks English gooder; more well*
points.sources: Murphy 105 · TE A2: Comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs · EGP: B1 (comparative clauses with adverbs)

points.name: Less … than, the least; than me / than I am
points.can_do: Compares downwards and finishes the comparison naturally: less expensive than, the least interesting; She's taller than me / than I am.
points.typical_errors: *lesser expensive; the less interesting of all; taller than I* (very formal); *less cheaper*
points.sources: Murphy 105, 107 · TE B1: Comparative and superlative adjectives and adverbs · EGP: B1 comparative clauses: finite after than

points.name: How big is the difference: much, a lot, far, a bit, slightly + comparative
points.can_do: Strengthens or softens a comparison: much cheaper, a lot more expensive, a bit colder, slightly better; never very + comparative.
points.typical_errors: COMPARE: *very cheaper; more cheaper; much more cheap; a lot of better*
points.sources: Murphy 106 · TE B2: Modifying comparatives · EGP: B1 with (so) much, with a (little) bit, with even; B2 with slightly, with a lot · Level: taught by the app from B1 (EGP B1); the list names it at B2

points.name: By far the best, nowhere near as … as, twice as … as, not nearly as
points.can_do: Modifies superlatives and as … as: by far the biggest, easily the best, nearly as good as, three times as expensive as.
points.typical_errors: *by far better; twice more expensive than; not near as good; three times so expensive*
points.sources: Murphy 106, 107 · TE B2: Modifying comparatives · EGP: B2 superlatives with by far

points.name: The sooner, the better; more and more
points.can_do: Shows that two things change together, or that something keeps changing: The more you practise, the easier it gets. It's getting colder and colder.
points.typical_errors: *More you practise, easier it gets; The more you practise, it gets easier; more and more cold; the more sooner*
points.sources: Murphy 106 · TE B1+: The … the … comparatives · EGP: B1 combining comparative adjectives with and; B2 the more … the more …

points.name: So + adjective, such (a) + noun
points.can_do: Makes a description stronger with the right word: so long, so quickly; such a long film, such nice people, such bad weather.
points.typical_errors: *so a long film; such long; such a nice people; a such good idea; so nice people*
points.sources: Murphy 102 · TE B1: So, such, so much, so many · EGP: B1 such (a) + adjective + noun

points.name: So much, so many
points.can_do: Uses so much with uncountable and so many with plural nouns: so much noise, so many people.
points.typical_errors: *so much people; so many traffic; such many people; so much of noise*
points.sources: Murphy 102 · TE B1: So, such, so much, so many · EGP: A2 so many with plural nouns; B1 so much, too much with uncountable nouns

points.name: So … that, such … that: the result
points.can_do: Adds the result of a strong quality: It was so cold that we stayed inside. It was such a cold day that we stayed inside.
points.typical_errors: *It was too cold that we stayed inside; so cold as we stayed; such cold that*
points.sources: Murphy 102 · TE B1+: So, such · EGP: B1 so + adjective + that clause; subordinated clauses: purpose, result · The app has these tasks from B1.1

points.name: Basic word order: subject, verb, object, place, time
points.can_do: Builds a statement in the fixed English order: I play tennis in the park on Sundays.
points.typical_errors: ADV-PLACE: *In my town is a park; I like very much tennis; Plays he tennis; Yesterday went I to work*
points.sources: Murphy 109 · TE A1: Basic word order · EGP: A1 declarative clauses; adverbs: time, place, end position

points.name: And, but, or
points.can_do: Joins words and sentences that add, contrast or give a choice; uses or after a negative: I don't eat meat or fish.
points.typical_errors: *I don't eat meat and fish; I like tea but coffee; and too I like*
points.sources: TE A1: And, but, or, so, because · EGP: A1 coordinating: word + word, clause + clause; but, concessive · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: So or because: result or reason
points.can_do: Gives the result with so and the reason with because: It was late, so we left. We left because it was late.
points.typical_errors: *I went home so the shop was closed; Because it was late, so we left; We left, because it was late*
points.sources: TE A1: And, but, or, so, because · EGP: A1 because, reasons; A2 so · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: The same kind of words on both sides: cooking and reading
points.can_do: Keeps the forms equal after and / or and leaves out the repeated subject: She got up and left. I like cooking and reading.
points.typical_errors: *I like cooking and read; She got up and she leaving; to walk or taking the bus*
points.sources: TE A2: However, although, because, so, time connectors (no line of its own) · EGP: A1 clause + clause, ellipted subject; B1 combining clauses of the same type · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: However, although, but
points.can_do: Contrasts two ideas in one sentence (although, but) or in two (However, …) with the right punctuation.
points.typical_errors: CONTRAST: *Although, it was late, we stayed; Although it was late, but we stayed; I'd love a dog, however my flat is small*
points.sources: Murphy 113 · TE A2: However, although, because, so, time connectors · EGP: A2 subordinating conjunctions, simple; B1 discourse markers: contrasting

points.name: Time connectors: then, after that, before, after, while, when
points.can_do: Orders the events of a story and puts a comma after a time clause that comes first: Before I go to bed, I read. Then I made breakfast.
points.typical_errors: *I had a shower. After, I made breakfast; After I made breakfast; Before go to bed, I read*
points.sources: TE A2: However, although, because, so, time connectors · EGP: A2 subordinated clauses: time; B1 discourse markers: sequencing · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Purpose: to + verb, for + noun
points.can_do: Says why somebody does something: I went to the bank to get some money. We stopped for a coffee.
points.typical_errors: *I went to the bank for get some money; for to get; for getting money* (purpose of an action)
points.sources: Murphy 64 · TE A2: Purpose with to and for · EGP: A2 subordinated clauses: purpose · The app has it at B1.1 and above

points.name: Because or because of; due to + noun
points.can_do: Uses because before a clause and because of / due to before a noun: because it snowed / because of the snow.
points.typical_errors: CONTRAST: *The flight was late because the snow; because of it snowed; He was late because the traffic*
points.sources: Murphy 113 · TE B1: Clauses of contrast, purpose and reason · EGP: B1 subordinated clauses: reason

points.name: Although, even though + clause; despite, in spite of + noun / -ing
points.can_do: Chooses the word by what follows: Although it was raining, we went out. Despite the rain / Despite feeling ill, …
points.typical_errors: CONTRAST: *Despite it was raining; Despite of the rain; even she has a lot to do; In spite the rain; Although the rain*
points.sources: Murphy 113 · TE B1: Clauses of contrast, purpose and reason; B1+: Clauses of contrast and purpose · EGP: B1 subordinated clauses: contrast; B2 complex subordinating conjunctions (despite)

points.name: So that + can / could / would
points.can_do: Gives a purpose with its own subject: I wrote it down so that I wouldn't forget. Speak slowly so that everyone can understand.
points.typical_errors: *so that I don't forgot; for that everyone understands; so everyone to understand; so that to understand*
points.sources: Murphy 64 · TE B1: Clauses of contrast, purpose and reason; B1+: Clauses of contrast and purpose · EGP: B1 subordinated clauses: purpose, result

points.name: As and since for a reason
points.can_do: Gives a reason the listener already knows: As it was late, we took a taxi. Since you're here, let's start.
points.typical_errors: *As it was late, so we took a taxi; Since it was late, that we took*
points.sources: Murphy 116 · TE B1: Clauses of contrast, purpose and reason · EGP: B1 subordinated clauses: reason

points.name: During, for, while
points.can_do: Uses during + noun (when), for + a period (how long), while + clause: during the film, for two hours, while we were watching.
points.typical_errors: *During I was cooking; during two hours; while the film; for the film I fell asleep*
points.sources: Murphy 119 · TE B1: During, for, while · EGP: B1 subordinating conjunctions, simple

points.name: By or until; by the time
points.can_do: Uses until for something that continues up to a moment and by for something that happens not later than it: Stay until five. Finish it by five.
points.typical_errors: *Finish it until five; Wait here since I come back; I'll be home until six* meaning not later
points.sources: Murphy 120 · TE no line of its own (B1: During, for, while) · EGP: C1 present simple with by the time

points.name: For, since, from … to
points.can_do: Uses for + a length of time, since + a starting point up to now, from … to for a finished period: from 2010 to 2014.
points.typical_errors: DURATION: *I've lived here from 2015; since three years; for 2015; I worked there since 2010 to 2014*
points.sources: Murphy 12 · TE B1: For, since, from · EGP: A2 for; B1 since · Overlaps the present perfect points; listed because the list has it as a lesson

points.name: On time / in time, at the end / in the end
points.can_do: Separates punctual (on time) from early enough (in time), and the last part (at the end of) from finally (in the end).
points.typical_errors: *in the end of the film; at the end we decided; I arrived on time to catch* for *in time*
points.sources: Murphy 122 · TE A2: On time / in time, at the end / in the end · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: In case
points.can_do: Takes a precaution: I'll take some cash in case the card machine isn't working; separates it from if.
points.typical_errors: TIME-CLAUSE: *in case it will rain; in case of it rains; I'll take an umbrella if it rains* (= only then)
points.sources: Murphy 114 · TE B2: Clauses of contrast, purpose, reason and result · EGP: B2 complex subordinating conjunctions

points.name: Whereas, while, nevertheless, yet, even so
points.can_do: Compares two facts (whereas, while) and concedes a point between sentences (Nevertheless, …).
points.typical_errors: *Whereas it was late, we stayed* for although; *It was late, nevertheless we stayed* (punctuation); *Despite, we stayed*
points.sources: Murphy 113 · TE B2: Clauses of contrast, purpose, reason and result · EGP: B2 discourse markers: comparing; C1 yet, concessive

points.name: In order to, so as not to, in order for … to, for + -ing
points.can_do: Gives a purpose formally, in the negative and with a new subject: so as not to wake her; in order for the plan to work; a tool for cutting metal.
points.typical_errors: *for not to wake her; in order to not; This tool is for cut metal; in order that the plan to work*
points.sources: Murphy 64 · TE B2: Clauses of contrast, purpose, reason and result · EGP: B2 complex subordinating conjunctions (in order that)

points.name: Owing to, on account of; therefore, consequently, as a result
points.can_do: Gives reasons and results in formal writing with the right structure and punctuation.
points.typical_errors: *owing the fog; due to it was foggy; Sales fell, therefore we closed* (comma splice); *as a result of we closed*
points.sources: TE B2: Clauses of contrast, purpose, reason and result; B2: Discourse markers · EGP: B2 discourse markers: summarising, formal · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Like or as
points.can_do: Uses like + noun for similarity and as + noun for a role, as + clause: She works as a teacher. She sings like a professional. Do as I say.
points.typical_errors: *She works like a teacher* (that is her job); *as my brother, I love football; Do like I say* (informal)
points.sources: Murphy 117 · TE no line in the lists · EGP: A2 be like + noun; B1 linking verb + like · Standard point from Murphy unit 117; no list line

points.name: Discourse markers: in fact, on the other hand, as far as I know, anyway
points.can_do: Organises speech and writing: adding, contrasting, giving an opinion, changing the subject.
points.typical_errors: *In the other hand; According to me; At the end* for finally; *As far I know*
points.sources: TE B2: Discourse markers · EGP: B1 organising: adding, contrasting, sequencing; B2 summarising, formal · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Defining relative clauses: who, which, that as the subject
points.can_do: Says which person or thing is meant: the woman who lives next door, a phone that takes good photos.
points.typical_errors: REL-WHICH: *the woman which lives; the book what I bought; the man who he called; the people who lives*
points.sources: Murphy 92 · TE A2: Defining relative clauses · EGP: A2 defining, subject, with who / which · Level: test-english A2, EGP A2; the app has the topic at B1.1-B1.2. Decided by the teacher, 13 November: A2.2, as in the list; A2.2 tasks are to be written.

points.name: Who, which, that as the object; leaving the word out
points.can_do: Leaves out the relative word when it is the object and never repeats the object: the film (that) we saw.
points.typical_errors: *The book that I bought it is great; the man who I met him; the film what we saw*
points.sources: Murphy 93 · TE B1: Defining and non-defining relative clauses · EGP: A2 defining, object, with that; defining, without pronoun

points.name: Where, whose, when
points.can_do: Adds a place, an owner or a time: the restaurant where we met, a driver whose car was stolen, the day when we met.
points.typical_errors: *the man who's car was stolen; the restaurant which we met; the man that his car; the city where I was born in*
points.sources: Murphy 94 · TE B1: Defining and non-defining relative clauses · EGP: B1 with where, place; with whose name; B2 defining with whose

points.name: What = the thing that
points.can_do: Uses what without a noun before it and that / which after a noun: I didn't hear what he said. Everything that he said was true.
points.typical_errors: REL-WHICH: *The book what I bought; Everything what he said; I didn't hear that he said*
points.sources: Murphy 93 · TE no line of its own (B1: Defining and non-defining relative clauses) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: Non-defining relative clauses: commas, who / which, never that
points.can_do: Adds extra information between commas: My brother, who lives in Berlin, is a nurse.
points.typical_errors: REL-WHICH: *My brother, that lives in Berlin; My brother who lives in Berlin, is a nurse* (one comma); *a presentation, that made*
points.sources: Murphy 95 · TE B1: Defining and non-defining relative clauses · EGP: A2 non-defining, subject, with who / which; B1 non-defining, object, with who

points.name: , which = the whole idea before it
points.can_do: Comments on a whole sentence: He didn't call, which was strange.
points.typical_errors: REL-WHICH: *He didn't call, what was strange; She worked in a hospital, what means; …, that was strange*
points.sources: Murphy 96 · TE B2: Defining and non-defining relative clauses · EGP: B2 sentence relative, evaluative · On the relative_clauses card only as a Watch out point

points.name: Prepositions in relative clauses: the man I was talking to / to whom
points.can_do: Puts the preposition at the end in everyday English and before whom / which in formal English.
points.typical_errors: REL-ORDER: *the man who about I was telling you; the house I live; the man to who I spoke; the hotel which we stayed*
points.sources: Murphy 93, 96 · TE B2: Defining and non-defining relative clauses · EGP: A2-B1 preposition stranding; B2 pronoun + preposition; preposition + wh- word · On the relative_clauses card only as a Watch out point

points.name: All of whom, most of which, neither of whom
points.can_do: Adds a quantity to a non-defining clause: She has three brothers, all of whom live abroad.
points.typical_errors: *all of them live abroad* (joined with a comma); *all of who; most of that*
points.sources: Murphy 96 · TE B2: Defining and non-defining relative clauses (from memory) · EGP: C1 quantity pronouns with relative pronouns

points.name: -ing and -ed clauses after a noun: the woman talking to Tom, the boy injured in the accident
points.can_do: Shortens a relative clause with a participle: active → -ing, passive → third form.
points.typical_errors: *the woman talked to Tom; the boy injuring in the accident; the people who waiting*
points.sources: Murphy 97 · TE B2: Participle clauses · EGP: B1-B2 subordinated: non-finite with -ing; C1 non-finite with -ed clauses

points.name: Participle clauses for time and reason: Feeling tired, I went to bed. Having finished, …
points.can_do: Replaces a clause with when / because / after by a participle, with the same subject in both parts.
points.typical_errors: *Walking down the street, a car hit me* (different subjects); *Having finish; Being tired, so I went to bed*
points.sources: Murphy 68 · TE B2: Participle clauses · EGP: B2 -ing clause; C1 not + -ing clause; C1 non-finite -ed clauses, focus · Level: test-english B2 and again C1 (Advanced participle clauses)

points.name: At, in, on: time
points.can_do: Uses at with clock times, on with days and dates, in with months, years, seasons and parts of the day; at night, at the weekend.
points.typical_errors: PREP-TIME: *in Monday; on 2020; at the morning; in night; on May*
points.sources: Murphy 121 · TE A1: At, in, on: time · EGP: A1 simple prepositions

points.name: No preposition: next Monday, last year, tomorrow, every day
points.can_do: Leaves out the preposition before next / last / this / every and tomorrow / yesterday.
points.typical_errors: *on next Monday; in last year; at this weekend; in every day; on tomorrow*
points.sources: Murphy 121 · TE A1: At, in, on: time · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: At, in, on: place
points.can_do: Uses in for inside and areas, on for surfaces, at for a point or a place of activity: in the fridge, on the wall, at the bus stop, at work.
points.typical_errors: *The keys are at the table; in the wall; on the fridge; in the bus stop; in work*
points.sources: Murphy 123, 124, 125 · TE A1: At, in, on: place · EGP: A1 simple prepositions

points.name: Next to, under, between, behind, in front of, opposite
points.can_do: Describes where things are in relation to each other.
points.typical_errors: *in front the house; between of; opposite of the bank; near of; behind of*
points.sources: TE A1: Next to, under, between… · EGP: A2 complex prepositions · Not a Murphy EGiU unit

points.name: Movement: to, into, out of, across, through, along, past; arrive in / at
points.can_do: Describes direction and says arrive in a city, arrive at a place, get to, go home: She walked into the room. We arrived in Riga.
points.typical_errors: *We arrived to Riga; go to home; enter into the room; I've been in Paris twice* (visit)
points.sources: Murphy 126 · TE A2: Prepositions of movement · EGP: A2 simple prepositions (increasing range)

points.name: By car, on the bus, in a taxi, on foot
points.can_do: Says how somebody travels: by bus, by train; on the bus, in the car; on foot.
points.typical_errors: *with bus; by foot; in the bus; on a taxi; by my car*
points.sources: Murphy 127, 128 · TE no line of its own (A2: Prepositions of movement) · EGP: A1 preposition + no article

points.name: Everyday verbs with their prepositions: listen to, look at, wait for, talk to
points.can_do: Uses the fixed preposition after the most common verbs and puts the object pronoun after it: Listen to me. I'm waiting for you.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *I'm waiting you; Listen me; Look me; She talked with me about* (fine) but *She told with me*
points.sources: Murphy 132, 133 · TE no line in A1-A2 (B1: Verb + preposition) · EGP: A1 prepositional verbs: verb + preposition + object · Taught by the app from A2.1; the list has verb + preposition only at B1

points.name: Verbs with no preposition: call me, discuss it, answer the question, join the team
points.can_do: Puts the object directly after these verbs: We discussed the plan. She married a doctor. Enter the room.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *discuss about the plan; call to me; join to our group; answer to the question; helped to other workers; married with*
points.sources: Murphy 132 · TE no line of its own (B1: Verb + preposition) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: Verb + preposition: depend on, belong to, apologise for, think about / of
points.can_do: Uses the right preposition after a wider range of verbs, also before -ing: It depends on the weather. She succeeded in passing.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *It depends from the weather; I dreamt with you; consists from; think on; Hope to hear you soon*
points.sources: Murphy 132, 133, 134, 135, 136 · TE B1: Verb + preposition · EGP: B1 prepositional verbs (increasing range)

points.name: Adjective + preposition: good at, afraid of, interested in, married to
points.can_do: Uses the right preposition after an adjective, also before -ing: I'm tired of waiting. She's good at maths.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP / ED-ING: *responsible about; interested about; good in; married with; afraid from; different of; I'm very interesting in*
points.sources: Murphy 130, 131 · TE B1: Adjective + preposition · EGP: A2 adjectives with prepositional phrase

points.name: Noun + preposition: a reason for, an increase in, a solution to
points.can_do: Uses the right preposition after a noun: the cause of, a rise in prices, a need for, an answer to.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *the reason of; an increase of prices* (amount aside); *a solution of the problem; the cause for; an answer on*
points.sources: Murphy 129 · TE B2: Noun + preposition · EGP: B1 noun + prepositional phrases

points.name: There and it as preparatory subjects
points.can_do: Starts a sentence with it for a clause and with there for existence: It's no use complaining. It's a pity that … There seems to be a problem. There's no point in waiting.
points.typical_errors: IT-THERE: *Is important to check; It seems to be a problem; There is important to; It is no point in waiting*
points.sources: Murphy 84 · TE B2: There and it as preparatory subjects · EGP: B1 it + be + adjective + that clause; there + modal verbs; B2 there + verbs with modal meaning

points.name: Have: auxiliary or main verb
points.can_do: Uses do with have as a main verb and have got for possession; separates have a shower (action) from have a car (state): Do you have …? I didn't have time. I'm having lunch.
points.typical_errors: *Had you a good time? I hadn't breakfast; I haven't time* (old-fashioned); *I'm having a car; Have you got a shower every day?*
points.sources: Murphy 17 · TE B2: Have: auxiliary or main verb · EGP: A2 auxiliary verbs have and do

points.name: Ellipsis and substitution: I think so, I hope not, do so, one / ones
points.can_do: Leaves out or replaces repeated words: A: Is it open? B: I think so. She said she would call, and she did. I prefer the red ones.
points.typical_errors: *I think yes; I hope no; I don't think it* for *I don't think so; She said she would call and she called it*
points.sources: Murphy 51 · TE B2: Ellipsis and substitution · EGP: B1 one, ones; B1 must, should: ellipsis; C1 none, substitution

points.name: Cleft sentences: It was Tom who …, What I need is …
points.can_do: Moves the important part forward for emphasis: It was the price that surprised me. What I need is a holiday. The thing that worries me is …
points.typical_errors: *It was Tom which called; What I need it is a holiday; It was yesterday when did I see him; What I need are a holiday*
points.sources: TE B2: Cleft sentences · EGP: B2 the thing / fact / point / problem is (that); C1 what cleft clause; C2 it cleft · Not in Murphy EGiU; Hewings, Advanced Grammar in Use (from memory, not checked) Level: test-english B2, EGP C1-C2. Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B2.2 is recognising the form and making it when the start is given; choosing and transforming is C1 (x_cleft_adv).

points.name: Inversion after negative adverbials: Never have I seen …, Not only … but also
points.can_do: Uses question word order after a fronted negative expression in formal style: Never have I seen such a mess. No sooner had we left than it started to rain.
points.typical_errors: *Never I have seen; Not only he came but also; No sooner we had left than; Hardly had we left than* (when)
points.sources: TE B2: Inversion with negative adverbials · EGP: B2 never, inverted front position; past perfect: inversion with no sooner … than; C1 not only … but also with inversion; C2 hardly … when · Not in Murphy EGiU; Hewings, Advanced Grammar in Use (from memory, not checked) Level: test-english B2; EGP B2 for never and no sooner, C1-C2 for the rest. Returns in C1: Advanced word order Decided by the teacher, 13 November: B2.2 is recognising the form and making it when the start is given; the full set and transformations are C1 (x_inv_neg, x_inv_main).

points.name: No article: I like cats. She drinks tea. He lives in Riga.
points.can_do: Uses no article with plural and uncountable nouns when speaking in general and with names of people, cities and most countries.
points.typical_errors: THE: *I like the cats* (all cats); *She drinks the tea every morning; He lives in the Riga*
points.sources: Murphy 75, 77 · TE A1: A / an, the, no article · EGP: A1 no article · The contrast with a particular group (children / the children) is `art_general` at B1.1

points.name: One and ones: the red one, Which ones?
points.can_do: Avoids repeating a countable noun: I'd like the blue one. Which ones are yours? This one is cheaper.
points.typical_errors: *I'd like the blue; Which are yours ones?; a one; I need some paper. Can you give me one?* (uncountable)
points.sources: TE B2: Ellipsis and substitution · EGP: A2 one; B1 ones, which one, this one · Not a Murphy EGiU unit (Hewings AGU 61). Level: EGP A2-B1; the list has it only inside B2: Ellipsis and substitution

points.name: What is she like? What does he look like? How is she?
points.can_do: Asks for a description with What … like? and about health or mood with How …?
points.typical_errors: *How is your new boss?* for a description; *How does he look like? What is she like?* answered *She likes tea*
points.sources: TE no line in the lists · EGP: A2 be like + noun or pronoun · Not a Murphy EGiU unit; a standard course-book point with no list line

points.name: Must or have to: my own view or somebody else's rule
points.can_do: Uses must when the speaker thinks it is necessary and have to for a rule or a situation, and prefers Do I have to …? to Must I …?
points.typical_errors: *I must wear a uniform at work* said about the company's rule; *Must I sign here?* in everyday speech
points.sources: Murphy 31 · TE B1: Have to, must, should · EGP: B1 must: obligation and necessity; have to · On the modal_verbs card as a Watch out point

points.name: Won't for refusing: The door won't open
points.can_do: Says that a person or a thing refuses to do something now: He won't listen. My laptop won't switch on.
points.typical_errors: *My laptop doesn't want to switch on; The door isn't opening* for a refusal
points.sources: Murphy 21 · TE no line of its own (returns in C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should) · EGP: A2 will: willingness; B1 would: willingness in the past · A Watch out point on the future card

points.name: Should for what we expect: She should be there by now
points.can_do: Says what is probably true or will probably happen because it is normal or planned: She left at six, so she should be there by now. The train should be here in five minutes.
points.typical_errors: *She must be there by now* where it is only an expectation; *The train should to be here*
points.sources: Murphy 33 · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen); no B2 line · EGP: B1 should: likelihood; B2 should: expectations · Level: Murphy treats it at intermediate level and EGP at B1-B2; test-english names it only on the C1 page

points.name: Both … and, either … or, neither … nor
points.can_do: Joins two things with a pair of words and keeps the verb positive after neither … nor: She speaks both French and German. You can either call or email. He neither smokes nor drinks.
points.typical_errors: DOUBLE-NEG / AGREE: *He doesn't neither smoke nor drink; Both she speaks French and German; Either you call or email*
points.sources: Murphy 89 · TE B1: Both, either, neither · EGP: B1 either … or; both … and with nouns; B2 neither … nor

points.name: Reporting verbs + that: admit, explain, complain, claim, warn somebody that
points.can_do: Reports with a that-clause and the tense one step back: She admitted that she had lost the file. He warned us that the road was closed.
points.typical_errors: SAY-TELL: *He explained me that; She complained me that; He warned that us; She admitted to lose the file*
points.sources: Murphy 34, 47, 48 · TE B1+: Reporting verbs · EGP: B2 reporting verbs (increasing range) · The app has the whole topic at B2.2

points.name: Need + -ing, help (to) do, can't help -ing; afraid to do / afraid of doing
points.can_do: Uses the patterns that do not follow the main lists: The car needs washing. She helped me (to) move. I couldn't help laughing. I'm afraid to tell him / afraid of making a mistake.
points.typical_errors: *The car needs to wash; She helped me moving; I couldn't help to laugh; I'm afraid of to tell him*
points.sources: Murphy 57, 66 · TE no line in the lists · EGP: B1 help + object · Standard point from Murphy units 57 and 66; no content and no list line

points.name: Fixed phrases with a preposition: on holiday, by mistake, at the age of, in my opinion
points.can_do: Uses the common fixed phrases as wholes: on business, on purpose, by chance, in a hurry, at first, for sale.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *in holiday; with mistake; in the age of 20; on my opinion; by purpose*
points.sources: Murphy 127, 128 · TE no line in the lists · EGP: A2-B1 complex prepositions · Close to vocabulary, like do / make; listed because Latvian uses other prepositions

points.name: The narrative present in stories, jokes and anecdotes
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Tells an informal story in the present to make it vivid: events in the present simple, the background in the present continuous: So I'm standing in the queue when this woman turns round and hands me her dog.
points.typical_errors: Mixes the two systems in one sentence (*So I stood in the queue and this woman hands me her dog*); uses the story present in a formal report
points.sources: AGU 2 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: B2 present simple: stories and commentaries

points.name: Live commentary, demonstrations and instructions
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Uses the present simple for actions described as they happen and for steps shown to somebody: Ozols wins the ball, turns and shoots. Now you fold the paper in half and press down.
points.typical_errors: *Ozols is winning the ball and is shooting* for quick completed actions in a commentary
points.sources: AGU 2 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: B2 present simple: stories and commentaries

points.name: Performative verbs: I admit, I apologise, I promise, I suggest
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Does the thing by saying it, in the present simple: I admit I was wrong. We apologise for the late reply; knows that in the negative some of these verbs may be continuous with no change (I don't suggest / I'm not suggesting you were careless).
points.typical_errors: *I'm admitting I was wrong; I'm thanking you for your help* said as the act itself
points.sources: AGU 1 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: B1-B2 present simple: speech act verbs

points.name: Headlines, summaries and the contents of books and films
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Reads and writes the present simple for recent events in headlines and for what a book, film or article says: Minister quits over tax claims. In the last chapter the author explains her method.
points.typical_errors: *Minister has quit / is quitting over tax claims* as a headline; *In the film a retired pilot was returning to his village*
points.sources: AGU 2 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: C1 present simple: reporting verbs

points.name: I hear, I gather, they say, Ilze tells me: news we have received
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Introduces something heard or read with a present reporting verb: I gather you've moved. Ilze tells me you're looking for a flat. They say the bridge will be closed all summer.
points.typical_errors: *I am hearing you've moved; I gather that you were looking for a flat* for a present situation
points.sources: AGU 2 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: C1 present simple: reporting verbs (wide range)

points.name: State verbs in the continuous: we're loving it, you're being very quiet
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Uses the continuous with be, like, love, look, sound for a temporary or changing state (We're loving the new office. You're being very quiet today) and keeps believe, consist of, doubt, own, belong, possess simple.
points.typical_errors: *The team is consisting of six people; I'm doubting it; This flat is belonging to my aunt*; *You are very quiet today* where the passing behaviour is the point
points.sources: AGU 1 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: B1 present continuous: temporary situations (the state-verb use is not a separate EGP entry) · Gold C1 reference, unit 1, Stative and dynamic verbs

points.name: Mental-state verbs in the continuous: I'm finding, I'm realising, she's regretting
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Shows that a thought or feeling has just started or is changing (find, think, realise, regret, understand): I'm realising how little time we have; keeps agree, believe, know, prefer simple.
points.typical_errors: *I'm knowing; I'm preferring tea these days; I'm agreeing with you*; *I realise* where the new, growing awareness is meant
points.sources: AGU 1 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: B1 mental process verbs with the present simple

points.name: The present continuous for politeness: I'm wondering whether …, We're hoping to …
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Softens a request or a plan: I'm wondering whether you could look at my draft. We're hoping to move in by May.
points.typical_errors: *I'm wondering can you look at my draft; I wonder that you could*; a bare *I hope you can look at it soon* to a senior person where the softer form is expected
points.sources: AGU 1 (modals with performatives) · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: C2 present continuous: politeness

points.name: Always, constantly, forever + continuous: characteristic behaviour; usually + continuous at a time
points.area: C1 · 1 Advanced present simple and continuous
points.can_do: Marks behaviour as typical, with irritation, surprise or approval (My neighbour is forever borrowing my ladder. She's always thinking of new ideas), and describes a routine in progress at a time (Don't ring at seven: we're usually putting the children to bed then).
points.typical_errors: *She constantly changes the plan!* is correct but loses the complaint; *We usually put the children to bed at seven* where 'in the middle of it' is meant
points.sources: AGU 2 · TE C1: Advanced present simple and present continuous (page seen) · EGP: B2, C2 present continuous with adverbs of indefinite frequency

points.name: Past continuous or past simple for two past activities: in progress or complete
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Chooses by emphasis when both are possible: While I was training as a nurse, I was sharing a flat (in progress) / When I trained as a nurse … (I finished the course).
points.typical_errors: Treats one of the two as wrong; *He was sitting down when the bell rang* for two events that follow each other
points.sources: AGU 4 · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (not in the part of the page seen) · EGP: C1 past simple: complex ordering of past events · Gold C1 reference, unit 2, Narrative tenses

points.name: Past continuous for repeated actions in a limited period
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Stresses that a repeated action belonged to a temporary period: During the audit we were staying late most evenings. While my car was being repaired, I was cycling to work every day.
points.typical_errors: *We were flying to Oslo four times last year* (a plain count needs the past simple)
points.sources: AGU 4 · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (page seen in part) · EGP: B1 past continuous: repeated events

points.name: Was always doing: irritation about a past habit
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Complains about what somebody kept doing: He was always leaving the lights on. She was forever criticising the food.
points.typical_errors: *He always left the lights on* is correct but neutral; *He was always leave; He had always leaving*
points.sources: AGU 2 (the present form); the past form is not in the units read · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (page seen in part) · EGP: A2-B1 past continuous with adverbs

points.name: Past forms for politeness: I was wondering if …, I wanted to ask …, We were hoping …
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Makes a present request more distant, and so more polite, with a past form: I was wondering if you might have a minute. I wanted to ask you about Friday.
points.typical_errors: *I had wondered if you might help* as a request now; answers *I wanted to ask …* as if it were about the past
points.sources: AGU 4 · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (page seen in part) · EGP: B2 past continuous: politeness; B2 past simple: politeness (I wondered, I wanted); C1 past simple: politeness (I thought)

points.name: Hopes and plans that came to nothing: was meaning to, had hoped, had expected
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Says what somebody intended or expected and did not get, with the past continuous or the past perfect: I was meaning to write, but the week got away from me. We had hoped the weather would hold.
points.typical_errors: *I was meaning write; We have hoped the weather would hold* about last week; *They expected a bigger crowd* where the disappointment is the point
points.sources: AGU 4, 5 · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (page seen in part) · EGP: B1-B2 future in the past · Gold C1 reference, Future in the past: advanced features

points.name: Past perfect or past simple when both are possible
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Uses the past perfect once to step back and then returns to the past simple, and knows that after, before and by the time often make it unnecessary: She had packed her bags and then called a taxi. After he locked / had locked the office, he went home.
points.typical_errors: Past perfect for every earlier action in a chain (*After I had got up I had made coffee and had left*); takes *After he locked the office* for a mistake
points.sources: AGU 5 · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (page seen in part) · EGP: B2 past perfect: change of situation; C1 past simple: complex ordering of past events · Gold C1 reference, unit 2, Narrative tenses

points.name: Past perfect (continuous) for a conclusion about what had happened; the cause of a past state
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Explains a past scene by what came before it: Someone had obviously moved the files. He was hoarse because he had been shouting all afternoon.
points.typical_errors: *He was hoarse because he was shouting all afternoon* (he had stopped); *Someone has obviously moved the files* about a past moment
points.sources: AGU 5 (unit 7 is not in the uploaded text) · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (page seen in part) · EGP: B2 past perfect continuous: results; background information

points.name: Past perfect continuous, past perfect or past continuous
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Chooses among an activity up to a past moment (had been doing), its finished amount or a state (had done) and what was in progress at the moment itself (was doing), also where two are possible: I hadn't been working there long when the firm was sold.
points.typical_errors: *We had been knowing each other for years; She had been ringing three times before I answered*
points.sources: AGU 7 (title from memory: the unit is not in the uploaded text) · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (not in the part of the page seen) · EGP: B2 past perfect continuous: results, background · Gold C1 reference, unit 2 (the practice contrasts these three forms)

points.name: Past forms that are not about the past: as if you were, I wish I had kept
points.area: C1 · 2 Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect
points.can_do: Uses a past form for something unreal now and a past perfect for something unreal then, after as if, wish, if only, would rather, it's time: You talk as if you owned the place. I wish I had kept the receipt.
points.typical_errors: *You talk as if you own the place* for something clearly untrue; *I wish I have kept the receipt; I wish I knew the answer earlier* about yesterday
points.sources: AGU 85 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: Advanced past simple, past continuous and past perfect (page seen in part) (exercise 1); C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen) · EGP: B1 past simple with wish; B2 past perfect after if only and wish · Gold C1 reference, Hypothetical meaning

points.name: The perfect in every time and form: have done, had done, will have done, to have done, having done
points.area: C1 · 3 The perfect tenses: forms and uses
points.can_do: Sees one meaning in all perfect forms, 'before a point in time', and uses the right one after modals, to and prepositions: He is thought to have left the country. She denied having read the letter.
points.typical_errors: *He is thought to left the country; She denied to have read it; After have eaten*
points.sources: AGU 3, 5, 6, 11 · TE C1: The perfect tenses: forms and uses (page seen) · EGP: C2 passives: non-finite perfect clauses and complements · Gold C1 reference, unit 1, Perfect aspect

points.name: This morning, today, this week: two correct sentences, two moments of speaking
points.area: C1 · 3 The perfect tenses: forms and uses
points.can_do: Reads from the tense when the sentence is said, and chooses it the same way: I didn't check my email this morning (said in the afternoon) / I haven't checked my email this morning (said at ten). At B1 the context decides; here both sentences are correct and the meaning differs.
points.typical_errors: Takes one of the two sentences for a mistake; one fixed tense for *today / this week*, whatever the moment of speaking
points.sources: AGU 3 · TE C1: The perfect tenses: forms and uses (page seen; this point is not on it) · EGP: B1 present perfect: unfinished

points.name: Tenses with since: Since she joined … have doubled; since I've had this job
points.area: C1 · 3 The perfect tenses: forms and uses
points.can_do: Uses the past simple in the since-clause for a point in the past and the present perfect there when both situations still continue: Since she joined the team, sales have doubled. I haven't slept well since I've had this job.
points.typical_errors: *Since she has joined the team, sales doubled; Since I have this job I didn't sleep well*
points.sources: AGU 3 · TE C1: The perfect tenses: forms and uses (page seen) · EGP: B1 present perfect: duration with since

points.name: The moment / once / by the time + present perfect for the future, + past simple for the past
points.area: C1 · 3 The perfect tenses: forms and uses
points.can_do: Refers to the future with the present perfect in the time clause and to the past with the past simple: Text me the moment you've landed. The moment we landed, I texted her. Once you've paid, the order can't be changed.
points.typical_errors: *Once you paid, the order can't be changed; I'll text you the moment I landed*
points.sources: AGU 3 · TE C1: The perfect tenses: forms and uses (page seen) · EGP: C1 present simple with by the time

points.name: It's the second time he has …; it was the first time I had …
points.area: C1 · 3 The perfect tenses: forms and uses
points.can_do: Keeps the perfect after It / This / That is (was) the first time, with the tense that matches: It's the second time he has missed the deadline. It was the first time I had spoken in public.
points.typical_errors: *It was the first time I spoke in public; This is the first time I am seeing snow*
points.sources: AGU 3 · TE C1: The perfect tenses: forms and uses (page seen) · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: Present perfect continuous or simple: repeated actions, changes, amounts
points.area: C1 · 3 The perfect tenses: forms and uses
points.can_do: Uses the continuous for an activity or repeated action up to now and the simple for a result, a number or a state, also where both are possible with a difference of emphasis: I've been ringing the bank all morning / I've rung the bank four times. Rents have been going up for years / have gone up by 8 per cent.
points.typical_errors: *I've been ringing the bank four times; Rents have been going up by 8 per cent; I've been having this phone since May*
points.sources: AGU 6 · TE C1: The perfect tenses: forms and uses (page seen) · EGP: B1 present perfect continuous: repeated continuing events; B2 recent past · Gold C1 reference, unit 1, Present perfect simple and continuous

points.name: Perfect simple or continuous in the past and the future as well
points.area: C1 · 3 The perfect tenses: forms and uses
points.can_do: Carries the same choice into every time: She had painted the fence before the rain came / She had been painting all morning, so her arms ached. By May I'll have taught here for ten years / I'll have been teaching here for ten years.
points.typical_errors: *By May I'll have been knowing her for ten years; She had been painting two rooms before lunch; By next week she will work on the project for six months*
points.sources: AGU 6, 11 (unit 7 is not in the uploaded text) · TE C1: The perfect tenses: forms and uses (page seen) · EGP: B2 future perfect continuous: looking back from a point in the future; B2 past perfect continuous

points.name: Will and would for characteristic behaviour and for what is always true
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Describes what is typical now with will and what was typical with would, never one particular occasion: Our cat will sit at the window for hours. Wood will float. As students we would cook together every Sunday.
points.typical_errors: *Last night he would cook dinner* (one occasion); *The cat will sit there for hours* understood as a prediction; *I would be very shy as a child* (a state needs used to)
points.sources: AGU 16 · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: C1 will: habitual and typical; B2 would: habitual past

points.name: Will, won't and wouldn't to criticise a habit; if you will …
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Criticises what somebody typically does or did: She will interrupt when I'm on the phone! He won't listen to advice. 'I've got a headache.' 'Well, if you will stare at a screen all night …'
points.typical_errors: 'Corrects' *if you will stare at a screen* to *if you stare* and loses the criticism; reads *She will interrupt* as a prediction
points.sources: AGU 16 · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: C2 will: willfulness or disapproval

points.name: Will for an assumption: That'll be the courier. He'll have heard by now.
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Draws a confident conclusion about the present with will (be doing) and about the past with will have done: Don't ring now: they'll be having lunch. He'll have heard the news by now.
points.typical_errors: *He will hear the news by now; They will have lunch now* as a guess about this moment; every *will have done* read as future
points.sources: AGU 16 · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: C1 future perfect simple: assumptions; C2 future perfect continuous: assumptions

points.name: Would have done without if: an imagined past
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Says what would have happened in other circumstances, with the condition left unsaid: I would have come, but nobody told me. I'd have chosen the blue one.
points.typical_errors: *I will have come, but nobody told me; I would come yesterday, but I was busy; I had come, but*
points.sources: AGU 16 · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: B1 would: imagined situations in the past

points.name: Wouldn't for refusal on one occasion
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Uses won't and wouldn't for refusal, also of things and also on one occasion, where positive would is not possible: The printer wouldn't work this morning. She wouldn't sign.
points.typical_errors: *She would sign the form yesterday* meaning she agreed once; *The printer didn't want to work*
points.sources: AGU 16 · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: B1 would: willingness in the past

points.name: Would for distance: I'd say, I'd have to disagree, I would have thought
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Makes an opinion less direct: I'd say that's about right. I'd have to disagree there. I would have thought the earlier train was safer.
points.typical_errors: *I will say that's about right; I would to say; I would thought*
points.sources: AGU 16 (not in the part of the unit read) · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: B1 would: indirectness; C1-C2 would with adverbs

points.name: Should for a logical conclusion; should have: expectation or criticism
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Concludes from what is known (Forty chairs should be enough) and reads should have done both ways: The parcel should have arrived by now (I expect so) / You should have phoned (you did not).
points.typical_errors: Every *should have done* read as criticism; *Forty chairs must be enough* where it is only a calculation
points.sources: AGU 20 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: B1 should: likelihood; B2 should: expectations · Gold C1 reference, Modal verbs

points.name: If you will / would …; if you should …; Should you …
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Uses will or would after if for willingness or a polite request and should for a small chance, with or without inversion: If you will follow me, I'll show you the room. If you should change your mind, call me. Should you change your mind, …
points.typical_errors: Rejects every *will* after *if*; *If you would change your mind, call me; Should you will change your mind*
points.sources: AGU 83, 84 · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: C1 if + should, formal, polite; C1 inverted conditional with should · Gold C1 reference, Conditionals: advanced features

points.name: So that … should, in case … should (formal)
points.area: C1 · 4 Advanced modals: will, would, should
points.can_do: Uses should in formal purpose clauses and after in case for a small chance: He spoke quietly so that he shouldn't wake the baby. Keep the receipt in case you should need it.
points.typical_errors: *so that he shouldn't to wake; in case you will need it; so that he doesn't woke*
points.sources: AGU 81 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: B1 subordinated clauses: purpose, result

points.name: Can and could for what is sometimes true
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Says that something happens sometimes or is typical: Winters here can be very long. My uncle could be quite stubborn.
points.typical_errors: *Winters here may be very long* for a known tendency; *It can be snowing now* for a guess about this moment
points.sources: AGU 15 · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: B1-B2 can: general truths and tendencies · Gold C1 reference, Modal verbs: Ability

points.name: Can or could: a real or a theoretical possibility; can't for impossible
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Uses can for what really happens or is quite possible and could for what is only theoretical or less likely: We can take the early ferry (it runs every day) / We could take the early ferry (if there is one); uses can't, not couldn't, for what is impossible now and can't have / couldn't have done for the past.
points.typical_errors: *Living alone can be lonely, I imagine* said by somebody who has never tried it (could); *That can be true* for a guess (could / may)
points.sources: AGU 15 · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: B2 can: guesses and predictions; C1 can: past negative, deductions

points.name: Can or be able to: where each is preferred; could with see, hear, remember
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Prefers can as we speak, before passives and for general ability, and uses could for one past moment with verbs of the senses and thinking and after hardly, almost, the only thing: These forms can be filled in online. I could hear the sea from my room.
points.typical_errors: *The forms are able to be filled in online; I was able to hear the sea; He could reach the summit at the third attempt* for one achievement
points.sources: AGU 15 · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: B1 be able to: past

points.name: Could or was allowed to: permission on one occasion
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Uses was allowed to, not could, for permission given once, and either form in the negative: We could stay up late on Saturdays (always). Last night the children were allowed to stay up.
points.typical_errors: *Last night the children could stay up till eleven* (= got permission once)
points.sources: AGU 15 · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: B1 could: permission; be allowed to

points.name: May or might: formal or everyday; no may in questions about possibility
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Prefers may in academic and formal language and might in speech, and asks Could …? or Is … likely to …? instead of May …?: The results may indicate a wider problem. I might pop round later. Could the figures be wrong? May stays in formal requests and offers: May I add something?
points.typical_errors: *May the figures be wrong? May she accept the offer?*
points.sources: AGU 17 · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: B2 may: formal uses; C1 might: questions

points.name: May / might … but: admitting a point before disagreeing
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Concedes one thing and stresses another: The flat may be small, but it's bright. She might not have much experience, but she learns fast.
points.typical_errors: *The flat can be small, but it's bright; She may not much experience; Maybe the flat is small, but* (weaker)
points.sources: AGU 17 · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: C2 may: concession

points.name: May well, might as well; You might have warned me
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Strengthens a possibility (They may well cancel the flight), suggests the only sensible thing (There's no bus, so we might as well walk) and reproaches (You might have warned me!).
points.typical_errors: *They may good cancel; We might as well to walk; You might warned me*
points.sources: AGU 17 (may / might have; the fixed phrases from memory) · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: C1 may well; C2 may as well, might as well; C1 might: polite criticism; C1 could: criticism

points.name: May / might be doing, may / might have been doing
points.area: C1 · 5 Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might
points.can_do: Talks about a possible activity in the future, now or in the past: This time next week I may be sitting on a beach. He might have been joking. By Friday I might have finished.
points.typical_errors: *I can be sitting on a beach next week* (not can); *He might been joking; He might have be joking*
points.sources: AGU 17 · TE C1: Advanced modals: can / be able to, may / might (page seen) · EGP: C1 future continuous: expectations with might or may

points.name: The present subjunctive: The board demanded that the director resign
points.area: C1 · 6 The subjunctive: present and past
points.can_do: Uses the base form for every person after demand, insist, recommend, propose, request, suggest (that), with not before it and be + third form in the passive: They insisted that she not be informed. We propose that the fee be reduced.
points.typical_errors: PATTERN: *The board demanded the director to resign; demanded that the director resigns* in a formal letter; *that she doesn't be informed*
points.sources: AGU 39 · TE C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen) · EGP: C1 present simple after speech act verbs expressing suggestions and obligation

points.name: That … should, the subjunctive or an ordinary tense: three levels of formality
points.area: C1 · 6 The subjunctive: present and past
points.can_do: Moves between The doctor recommended that she should rest (neutral, British), that she rest (formal) and that she rests (informal) and chooses by the situation.
points.typical_errors: Treats two of the three as mistakes; *recommended that she should to rest; recommended her that she rest*
points.sources: AGU 39 · TE C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen); C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: C1 should: after if clauses, inversion (the that-clause use is not a separate EGP entry)
