points.name: After it is vital / essential / important that …, and after nouns: the request that …
points.area: C1 · 6 The subjunctive: present and past
points.can_do: Uses the subjunctive or should after adjectives and nouns of necessity: It is vital that every guest sign the register. Our request that the meeting be postponed was refused.
points.typical_errors: *It is vital that every guest is signing the register* in a formal text; *It is important for that he comes*
points.sources: AGU 39 · TE C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen); C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: B1-B2 it + be + adjective + that clause

points.name: Should for a reaction: It's odd that she should say that
points.area: C1 · 6 The subjunctive: present and past
points.can_do: Shows surprise, regret or disbelief about a fact with should in the that-clause, and an ordinary tense in less formal style: I'm amazed that he should have forgotten.
points.typical_errors: A subjunctive here (*I'm amazed that he forget*): after reactions only should or an ordinary tense is possible
points.sources: AGU 39 · TE C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen); C1: Advanced modals: will, would, should (page seen) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: The past subjunctive: if I were, I wish it were, as if I were, if … were to
points.area: C1 · 6 The subjunctive: present and past
points.can_do: Uses were for all persons in unreal and formal contexts and were to for an unlikely future: If the bank were to refuse, we would sell the car. She speaks to me as if I were a child.
points.typical_errors: *If the bank would refuse; as if I am a child* for something untrue; *If I were to knew*
points.sources: AGU 85 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen) · EGP: C2 if it were + to-infinitive, formal; C2 inverted were + to-infinitive

points.name: I'd rather you had told me: the unreal past about the past
points.area: C1 · 6 The subjunctive: present and past
points.can_do: Regrets what somebody did with would rather / would sooner + past perfect, next to wish + past perfect: I'd rather you had told me before the meeting. I'd sooner she hadn't sold it.
points.typical_errors: *I'd rather you told me yesterday; I'd rather you wouldn't have sold it*
points.sources: AGU: no unit of its own (not checked) · TE C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen) (the past perfect for an unreal past; would rather + past perfect is not on the page) · EGP: not found in EGP · Gold C1 reference, Hypothetical meaning (would rather + past simple / + past perfect)

points.name: Fixed subjunctive phrases: be that as it may, so be it, come what may, suffice it to say
points.area: C1 · 6 The subjunctive: present and past
points.can_do: Understands and uses the set phrases that keep the old subjunctive.
points.typical_errors: Changes the phrase to an ordinary tense (*be that as it is; so is it*)
points.sources: Murphy not in the AGU units read · TE C1: The subjunctive: present and past (page seen) · EGP: not found in EGP

points.name: Long subjects: the main noun, together with …, a subject after the verb
points.can_do: Makes the verb agree with the main noun of a long subject, does not count a phrase with together with or as well as, and finds the subject when it follows the verb: The cost of the repairs was higher than expected. The manager, together with two assistants, is meeting the client. At the end of the corridor are two meeting rooms.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *The cost of the repairs were higher; The manager, together with two assistants, are meeting the client; At the end of the corridor is two meeting rooms*
points.sources: AGU 40 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: A clause as the subject; the subject, not the complement, decides
points.can_do: Uses a singular verb after an -ing clause, an infinitive or another clause as subject, either form after a what-clause before a plural noun, and makes be agree with the subject: Working night shifts affects your sleep. How they got in is still unclear. What we need is (are) more volunteers. The biggest cost is the salaries.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *Working night shifts affect your sleep; How they got in are unclear; The biggest cost are the salaries*
points.sources: AGU 40 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: One of the teachers who run …; the only teacher who runs …
points.can_do: Makes the verb in a relative clause agree with what who or which refers to: She is one of the teachers who run the club. She is the only teacher who runs a club.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *the only teacher who run a club; one of the teachers who runs the club* in careful writing
points.sources: AGU 41 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: Collective nouns: the jury has its … / have their …
points.can_do: Uses a singular verb and its for the group as a unit and a plural verb and their for its members, keeps the two apart in one sentence, and uses a plural verb with police, people and cattle: The jury has reached its verdict. The jury are taking their seats. The police have closed the road.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *The police has closed the road; The jury has taken their seats* (singular and plural mixed)
points.sources: AGU 40, 42 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: B1 collective nouns

points.name: Each of, none of, neither of; a number of / the number of; more than one; one in four
points.can_do: Knows where the singular is required, where the plural is, and where both are used: The number of applicants has fallen. A number of applicants have withdrawn. Neither of the lifts works (work). None of the luggage was lost; none of the passengers were hurt. More than one flat has been sold. One in four tenants pay late.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *The number of applicants have fallen; A number of applicants has withdrawn; Each of the flats have a balcony; More than one flat have been sold; None of the luggage were lost*
points.sources: AGU 41 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: C1 either, neither + of + determiner with plural noun

points.name: X and Y: two things or one; either … or, neither … nor: the nearest noun
points.can_do: Uses a plural verb after and unless the two are one person or one idea, a singular verb after every … and …, and after or / nor makes the verb agree with the last item: My colleague and best friend is leaving / My colleague and my best friend are leaving. Every chair and table was sold. Neither the manager nor her assistants were there.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *Her patience and her humour makes her a good teacher; Every chair and table were sold; Neither the assistants nor the manager were there* (careful style: was)
points.sources: AGU 41 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: B2 neither … nor; C1 either … or

points.name: Nouns with unexpected forms: politics is, the Netherlands is, this series is, the criteria are, a pair of glasses is
points.can_do: Uses a singular verb with subjects and activities in -s, with names and titles in the plural, a plural verb with criteria and phenomena, the same form for one or more series, species, means, and knows that data and media take both: Politics is in his blood. The Netherlands is a small country. Both series are worth watching. My glasses are broken, but this pair is new.
points.typical_errors: UNCOUNT: *The news are; Politics are a difficult subject; The Netherlands are a small country; The criteria is strict; This phenomena; This pair of glasses are new*
points.sources: AGU 40, 42 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: C1 uncountable nouns

points.name: Amounts, measurements, percentages and fractions
points.can_do: Uses a singular verb with an amount seen as one thing, a plural verb when the units are thought of separately, and makes the verb agree with the noun after a percentage or fraction: Twenty euros is too much for a sandwich. The last two winters have been mild. A third of the staff work from home; a third of the building is empty.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *Twenty euros are too much; Six kilometres are a long walk; A third of the flats is empty*
points.sources: AGU 42 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: There is / are with plurals; there's in speech
points.can_do: Makes be agree with the noun that follows, knows the informal There's + plural and avoids it in writing: There are several reasons for the delay.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *There is several reasons* in an essay; *There are a lot of noise; There's two messages for you* in a formal email
points.sources: AGU 41, 95 · TE C1: Subject-verb agreement: advanced rules (page seen) · EGP: C1 question tags with there + be

points.name: Preposition + whom / which, or the preposition at the end
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Puts the preposition before whom or which in formal style and at the end in everyday style, never before that or who, and keeps a phrasal verb together: the colleagues with whom she shares an office / the colleagues she shares an office with; a mistake I came across.
points.typical_errors: REL-ORDER: *the charity to that he left his money; the colleagues with who; the form in which I filled; the man who about I told you*
points.sources: AGU 55 · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (not in the part of the page seen) · EGP: B2 relative clauses: pronoun + preposition; C1 prepositions: formal · Gold C1 reference, Prepositions in relative clauses

points.name: Of which, of whose, none / most / both of which
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Uses noun + of which next to whose and adds a quantity before of which / of whom: a village the name of which I can't recall; three offers, none of which was acceptable; her sons, both of whom are doctors.
points.typical_errors: *three offers, none of them was acceptable* (written as one sentence); *both of who; the name of that*
points.sources: AGU 55 · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (not in the part of the page seen) · EGP: C1 quantity pronouns with relative pronouns

points.name: Formal noun + preposition + which: the extent to which, the basis on which, the way in which
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Uses the fixed formal combinations: The report shows the extent to which prices have risen. Nobody explained the basis on which the fee was set.
points.typical_errors: REL-ORDER: *the extent which prices have risen; the extent to that; the basis on what the fee was set; the way how it works*
points.sources: AGU 55 (these phrases are not in the unit text read) · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (page seen in part) · EGP: C1 prepositions: formal

points.name: The preposition stays in the passive: looked into, dealt with, accused of, objected to by
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Keeps the preposition of the verb after the passive form, also next to by: The complaint is being looked into. He was accused of lying. The plan was objected to by two members.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *The complaint is being looked; The matter has been dealt; He was accused for lying; The plan was objected by two members*
points.sources: Murphy not in the AGU units read · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (page seen in part) · EGP: B2 prepositional verb, stranded preposition

points.name: A preposition at the end of an infinitive: nobody to talk to, easy to work with
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Ends an infinitive clause with the preposition after a noun, a pronoun or an adjective, without repeating the object, and knows the formal form with which: She has nobody to talk to. This phone is easy to work with. We need a room in which to work.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *She has nobody to talk; We need a bigger table to work; This phone is easy to work with it; a room which to work in*
points.sources: Murphy not in the AGU units read · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (page seen in part) · EGP: A2-B1 preposition stranding

points.name: Multi-word prepositions: with a view to, in the event of, by means of, regardless of, with regard to
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Uses the formal prepositions of several words with a noun or -ing, also where to is a preposition: The road was closed with a view to repairing the bridge. In the event of rain, the concert moves indoors. Regardless of the cost, …
points.typical_errors: *with a view to repair the bridge; in the event of it rains; regardless the cost; in regard of your letter; by the means of*
points.sources: AGU 80, 81 (titles seen, text not read) · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (page seen in part) · EGP: B2 complex prepositions; C1 prepositions: formal

points.name: One verb, two prepositions, two meanings; verb + object + preposition
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Separates hear of / about / from, think of / about, throw to / at, care for / about, and uses the pattern with an object: The rain prevented us from leaving. They blamed the delay on the weather.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *I've never heard about this writer* (= of); *He threw the keys at me* meant kindly; *prevented us to leave; blamed me of the delay*
points.sources: AGU 92 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (not in the part of the page seen) · EGP: B2 verb + adverb + preposition; C2 phrasal-prepositional verbs with two objects

points.name: Prepositions after nouns; noun + preposition + -ing or noun + to
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Uses the preposition the noun requires and the right verb form after it: her talent for explaining, the advantage of living centrally, an attempt to escape, little hope of winning.
points.typical_errors: DEP-PREP: *the advantage to live centrally; an attempt of escaping; her talent in to explain; little hope to win*
points.sources: AGU 93 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (not in the part of the page seen) · EGP: B1 noun + prepositional phrases

points.name: After a preposition: -ing, a wh-clause or the fact that, never a bare that-clause
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Completes a preposition correctly: despite the fact that tickets were cheap; I'm curious about how it works; everything depends on whether she signs.
points.typical_errors: CONTRAST: *despite that tickets were cheap; curious about that it works; depends on if she signs; because of the tickets were cheap*
points.sources: AGU 86 (if and whether: title seen); the rest from memory · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (not in the part of the page seen) · EGP: B2 preposition + wh- word

points.name: Exception and alternative: apart from, except for, other than, in place of, besides, but for
points.area: C1 · 8 Prepositions: position and advanced patterns
points.can_do: Chooses the word for 'not including', 'in addition to' and 'without': Everyone voted except (for) the chairman. Nobody other than the owner has a key. Apart from Latvian, he speaks German. But for the delay, we would have caught the ferry.
points.typical_errors: *Except Latvian, he speaks German* meaning in addition; *apart of; other from the owner; but the delay we would have caught it*
points.sources: AGU 91 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: Prepositions: position and advanced patterns (page seen in part) (besides and but for are not on the page) · EGP: B2 complex prepositions; C1 prepositions: formal

points.name: The subject of a participle clause: the same as in the main clause
points.can_do: Writes participle clauses whose understood subject is the subject of the main clause and repairs those where it is not: Opening the envelope, she found two tickets.
points.typical_errors: *Opening the envelope, two tickets fell out; Having paid the bill, the waiter brought our coats; Walking home, it started to rain*
points.sources: AGU 58 · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: B2 -ing clause; C1 non-finite clauses · Gold C1 reference, Participle clauses

points.name: Past participle clauses for reason and condition: Built in the 1930s, …; Stored in a dry place, …
points.can_do: Starts a sentence with a passive participle: Built in the 1930s, the bridge is still in use. Stored in a dry place, the seeds keep for years. Asked about the delay, the minister gave no answer.
points.typical_errors: *Building in the 1930s, the bridge is still in use; Asking about the delay, the minister gave no answer* (he was asked)
points.sources: AGU 58 · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: C1 non-finite with -ed clauses, focus

points.name: Having done or doing; Having been done; Not knowing
points.can_do: Uses having + third form when the first action is complete or causes the second, the passive Having been …, and puts not before the participle: Having missed the last bus, we walked home. Having been warned about the traffic, they left early. Not knowing the area, I asked for directions.
points.typical_errors: *Having warned about the traffic, they left early* (they were warned); *Knowing not the area; Missing the last bus an hour earlier, we walked home*
points.sources: AGU 58 · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: C1 not + -ing clause; C2 non-finite perfect clauses · Gold C1 reference, Participle clauses

points.name: Absolute clauses: a participle clause with its own subject
points.can_do: Gives the clause a subject of its own in formal style, with an -ing form, a third form or having + third form: The weather being fine, we ate outside. The bridge closed for repairs, traffic went through the village. The last bus having gone, we walked. Weather permitting, the match starts at three.
points.typical_errors: *Being the weather fine, we ate outside; The weather been fine; The last bus having went*
points.sources: AGU 58 · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: C1 non-finite clauses

points.name: With + noun + participle: With prices going up, …; With the windows shut, …
points.can_do: Describes the circumstances with with, a noun and an -ing form (active, in progress), a third form (passive, a state) or having + third form (completed before): With prices going up, people are spending less. With the windows shut, the room was stuffy.
points.typical_errors: *With prices go up; With going up, people are spending less* (no subject); *With the windows shutting, the room was stuffy* (a state needs shut)
points.sources: AGU 59 · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: C1 non-finite clauses

points.name: There being …, There having been …
points.can_do: Says that something exists or is missing as the reason for the main clause: There being no questions, the chair closed the meeting. There having been two break-ins, the shop fitted an alarm.
points.typical_errors: *Being there no questions; There having no questions; It being no questions, the chair closed the meeting*
points.sources: Murphy not in the AGU units read · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: Comment phrases: Generally speaking, Judging by …, Considering …, Strictly speaking
points.can_do: Comments on the whole sentence with a fixed participle phrase, which does not need the subject of the main clause: Judging by the queue, the film is popular. Strictly speaking, the ticket is not valid.
points.typical_errors: *Generally spoken; Judged by the queue, the film is popular; Speaking general*; takes *Judging by the queue, the film …* for a participle with the wrong subject
points.sources: Murphy not in the AGU units read · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: B1 discourse markers: adverbs, stance

points.name: An -ing clause after the main clause for its result
points.can_do: Adds the direct consequence of the main clause: The river burst its banks, flooding the lower streets. The lift broke down, forcing everyone to use the stairs.
points.typical_errors: *The river burst its banks, flooded the lower streets; …, what flooded the lower streets; …, having flooded the lower streets*
points.sources: AGU 58 (the result use is not in the unit text read) · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: B2 -ing clause

points.name: On hearing, in trying, by booking, since changing, without locking
points.can_do: Chooses the preposition by meaning: on = when, in = as a result of doing, by = the method, without = a second action that does not happen: On hearing the alarm, leave the building. By booking early, we saved forty euros.
points.typical_errors: *On hear the alarm; By to book early; In booking early, we saved forty euros* (the method needs by); *Since changed jobs, I've slept better*
points.sources: AGU 59 · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: B1-B2 non-finite with -ing · Gold C1 reference, Other uses of participles

points.name: Conjunction + participle or adjective: when asked, once opened, if in doubt, though exhausted
points.can_do: Shortens a clause after when, while, if, although, once, unless: When asked for his name, he said nothing. Keep refrigerated once opened. Though exhausted, they kept walking.
points.typical_errors: *When asking for his name, he said nothing* (he was asked); *If it possible; Though being exhausted they kept walking*
points.sources: AGU 59 · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) · EGP: C1 non-finite after if; C2 non-finite after although, though

points.name: Participle or relative clause after a noun: where the short form is not possible
points.can_do: Shortens a relative clause for an action in progress, a state or a passive (the passengers waiting at gate 12, anyone wishing to speak, the candidates being interviewed) and keeps the full clause for a single finished action (the woman who rang this morning).
points.typical_errors: *The woman ringing this morning left a message; the candidates interviewing today* for those being interviewed
points.sources: from memory: the unit is not in the uploaded text · TE C1: Advanced participle clauses (page seen) (this point is not on the page) · EGP: B2 subordinated: non-finite with -ing; C1 passives: non-finite clauses

points.name: Inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials: the full set
points.can_do: Inverts the subject and the helping verb, adding do for a simple tense, after seldom, rarely, hardly … when, no sooner … than, not only, little, under no circumstances, only by …: Seldom have we had such a wet June. Not only did she win, she broke the record. At no time did anyone mention the price.
points.typical_errors: *Seldom we have had; Not only she won; No sooner we had arrived when; Under no circumstances you should leave the door open; Little they knew*
points.sources: AGU 100 · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: C1 not only … but also with inversion; C2 inversion with hardly … when · Gold C1 reference, Emphasis with inversion (negative adverbs; restrictive words and expressions)

points.name: Only when … / Not until … : inversion in the main clause
points.can_do: Leaves the first clause in normal order and inverts the second: Not until the guests had gone did we notice the stain. Only when the rain stops can we start.
points.typical_errors: *Not until had the guests gone we noticed the stain; Only when the rain stops we can start*
points.sources: AGU 100 · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: C2 present simple: inversion with only when

points.name: So … that, Such … that, nor / neither at the start
points.can_do: Emphasises with So + adjective or Such + be and adds a negative with nor: So loud was the music that we couldn't talk. So fast did the queue grow that the doors opened early. Such was the demand that the site crashed. She didn't reply, nor did she return my call.
points.typical_errors: *So loud the music was that; Such the demand was that; nor she returned my call; neither she did*
points.sources: AGU 100 · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: C2 negative clause + nor, focus

points.name: Had …, Were … to, Should …; but for, had it not been for
points.can_do: Produces the formal conditionals without if in transformations, with the uncontracted negative, and the alternatives with but for: Had it not been for the fog, the flight would have landed on time. Were the factory to close, the town would lose 300 jobs.
points.typical_errors: *Hadn't we left late, we would have caught it; Were the factory close; Had it not been the fog; But for the fog the flight would land on time* (about the past)
points.sources: AGU 99, 85 · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen; this point is not on it) · EGP: C1 inverted conditional with should; C2 inverted past perfect; C2 were it not for; C2 had it not been for · Gold C1 reference, Conditionals: formal style

points.name: Here comes …, Out went …, At the top of the hill stands …
points.can_do: Puts the verb before a noun subject after here / there, an adverb of direction or a place phrase, and keeps normal order with a pronoun: Here comes our taxi. Here it comes. Out went the lights.
points.typical_errors: *Here comes it; Out did go the lights; Here our taxi comes* said as the announcement
points.sources: AGU 99 · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: B1 fronting, adverbs; A2 fronting, prepositional phrases

points.name: As and than + inversion in formal comparison
points.can_do: Recognises and writes inversion after as and than with a noun subject: The west of the country voted yes, as did most of the capital. City dwellers spend more on rent than do people in villages.
points.typical_errors: *than do they* (no inversion with a pronoun); *as most of the capital did too* in a formal text where the inverted form is expected
points.sources: AGU 99 · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen; this point is not on it) · EGP: not a separate EGP entry

points.name: Advanced cleft sentences: What he did was …, All we need is …, It was only when … that
points.can_do: Focuses an action, a single thing or a time clause: What he did was (to) resign. All we need is a signature. The reason I called was that the invoice is wrong. What happened was that the server crashed. It was only when I saw the bill that I understood.
points.typical_errors: *What he did was resigned; All what we need is; It was only when I saw the bill when I understood; The reason I called is because of*
points.sources: AGU 98 (title seen, text not read) · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: C1 what cleft clause; C2 wh- cleft with how / why / where; C2 it cleft

points.name: Fronting an object or a clause: That offer I turned down at once
points.can_do: Moves an object or a clause to the front for contrast or to link with what was said, with normal subject and verb order after it: That offer I turned down at once. The first flat we liked; the second we couldn't afford.
points.typical_errors: *That offer I turned it down; That offer did I turn down at once* (no inversion here)
points.sources: Murphy not in the AGU units read · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: C1 fronting: fixed expressions; C2 multiple fixed expressions

points.name: Fronting with as and though: Cold though it was, …; Much as I like …; Try as she might, …
points.can_do: Concedes a point formally with adjective or adverb + as / though, much as, and verb + as + subject + might: Cold though it was, we swam. Much as I like the idea, I can't afford it. Try as she might, she couldn't open it.
points.typical_errors: CONTRAST: *Cold though was it; Although cold it was; As much I like the idea; Try as she might, but she couldn't open it*
points.sources: AGU 82 (the unit is not in the uploaded text) · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: C2 non-finite after although, though

points.name: A participle or complement first, then be, then the subject: Waiting at the door was a courier
points.can_do: Starts with an -ing form, a third form or another complement of be and puts be before the subject, with agreement: Waiting at the door was a courier. Enclosed with this letter are two forms.
points.typical_errors: AGREE: *Enclosed with this letter is two forms; Waiting at the door a courier was*
points.sources: Murphy not in the AGU units read · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen) · EGP: C1 non-finite with -ed clauses, focus

points.name: Adverbs that change the meaning by their place: only, even, also; comment and viewpoint adverbs
points.can_do: Places only, even, just next to what they focus on and uses sentence adverbs in front or mid position: Only Anna signed the letter / Anna only signed the letter (she didn't write it). Frankly, I'm not surprised. Financially, it makes sense.
points.typical_errors: *I even didn't know his name; She has only seen him once* written where *only once* is the focus; *Financial, it makes sense*
points.sources: AGU 74, 75, 77, 78 (titles seen, text not read) · TE C1: Advanced word order (page seen; this point is not on it) · EGP: C2 adverbs: mid position, distancing
